name: Sirach (Ben Sira)
sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of Sirach (the Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach, Ecclesiasticus) as printed in H. B. Swete, *The Old Testament in Greek according to the Septuagint*, vol. 2 (1891; public domain), which follows Codex Vaticanus (B) with the readings of Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A) and others. The book was written in Hebrew by Jesus (Yeshua) son of Eleazar son of Sira in Jerusalem about 190–180 BC and translated into Greek in Egypt by his grandfather's grandson, as the translator's Prologue explains, after 132 BC. About two-thirds of the Hebrew has been recovered, as reported: six medieval manuscripts from the Cairo Geniza (MSS A–F, found from 1896 on), a scroll from Masada (1st century BC, covering 39:27–44:17), and from Qumran 2Q18 (2QSir, fragments of chapter 6) and the Psalms Scroll 11QPs-a (51:13–20 and the end of 51:30). Where these differ in substance from the Greek, the notes mention it, in general terms unless the reading has been checked. A longer Greek recension (“GII”), attested in some manuscripts and in the Latin, adds lines and whole verses; the verses that standard English Bibles number from GII but that are absent from Swete's text are given here in square brackets with a note, and other GII additions are given in the notes. In 30:25–36:16 the Greek manuscripts have two blocks of text transposed; this translation follows the order of the Hebrew, the Latin and English Bibles (NRSV numbering), as noted at 30:25 and 33:13. Sirach is received as Scripture by Catholic and Orthodox churches; Protestant churches place it among the Apocrypha. The Greek translator's Prologue is printed before chapter 1. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord” and *theos* “God.” Measures are given in US units with the original and metric values in the notes; dates are given as BC/AD. Variant readings not checked directly against the manuscripts are cited “as reported.” Brenton's English (1844) was consulted only as a check and not copied. CJT draft.

chapters.heading: Prologue of the Greek Translator
chapters.title: Many great things have been handed down to us through the Law and the Prophets and the other writers who came after them, and on their account Israel deserves praise for instruction and wisdom. Now it is right not only that those who read should themselves become learned, but that lovers of learning should be able, by speaking and by writing, to be of service to those outside. So my grandfather Jesus,{a} after devoting himself more and more to reading the Law and the Prophets and the other books of our ancestors, and after gaining a good command of them, was moved to write something of his own on matters of instruction and wisdom, so that those who love learning, once they had taken this in as well, might go much further in a life lived by the law. / You are urged, then, to read with goodwill and close attention, and to make allowance wherever, despite the care spent on the rendering, we may seem to fall short with some of the phrases. For what is said in Hebrew does not have the same force when it is carried over into another tongue. And not this book alone: the Law itself, the Prophecies, and the rest of the books differ not a little when they are read in their own language. / In the thirty-eighth year of King Euergetes{b} I came to Egypt and stayed some time, and I found a copy that gave no small instruction. I thought it most necessary to apply some zeal and labor of my own to translating this book. Through that span of time I brought much wakefulness and skill to the task of finishing the book and publishing it for those living abroad who wish to love learning and are training their ways to live by the law.

subheads.1: The Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach

verses.text:
All wisdom is from the Lord,
and it is with him to the age.

The sand of the seas, the drops of rain,
and the days of the age — who will number them out?

The height of heaven, the breadth of the earth,
the abyss, and wisdom — who will track them down?

Wisdom was created before all things,
and prudent understanding is from the age.

[The spring of wisdom is God's word on high,
and her paths are commands everlasting.]{c}

The root of wisdom — to whom has it been laid bare?
Her clever devices — who has come to know them?

[Wisdom's knowledge — to whom has it been shown?
Her rich experience — who has grasped it?]

There is One who is wise, exceedingly to be feared,
seated upon his throne —

upon all flesh, as he chose to give,
and he supplied her richly to those who love him.{d}

The fear of the Lord is glory and a ground for boasting,
gladness and a garland of exultation.

The fear of the Lord will delight the heart
and will give gladness and joy and long days.{e}

With the one who fears the Lord it will go well at the last;
on the day of his death he will find favor.{f}

The beginning of wisdom is to fear the Lord;
she was created with the faithful in the womb.

Among human beings she made her nest, a foundation from the age,
and among their offspring she will be held in trust.

To fear the Lord is wisdom's fullness;
she makes people drunk with her fruits.

She will fill her whole house with things to be desired,
and her storerooms with her produce.

The fear of the Lord is wisdom's garland,
making peace and sound health bloom.{g}

To fear the Lord is the root of wisdom,
and length of days are her branches.

[The fear of the Lord drives sins away,
and where it stays, it turns aside all anger.]

Unrighteous rage cannot be acquitted,{i}
for the swing of his rage is his ruin.

Until the right time the patient will hold out,
and later gladness will spring up for him.

Until the right time he will hide his words,
and the lips of many will tell out his good sense.

In wisdom's treasure chests are the proverbs of knowledge,
but reverence for God is a horror to the sinner.

If you crave wisdom, keep the commandments,
and the Lord will furnish her to you.

For the fear of the Lord is wisdom and instruction,
and what pleases him is faithfulness and mildness.

Do not be disobedient to the fear of the Lord,
and do not come to him with a doubled heart.

Do not act a part in people's mouths,{j}
and keep watch on your lips.

Do not raise yourself up, or you may fall
and bring dishonor on your own soul;
the Lord will lay bare your secrets
and hurl you down in the midst of the assembly,
because you did not draw near in the fear of the Lord,
and your heart was full of guile.

notes.text: Greek Iēsous, the Greek form of Joshua (Hebrew Yeshua). In 50:27 the author is called “Jesus son of Sirach son of Eleazar of Jerusalem”; Hebrew MS B there reads “Simeon son of Jeshua son of Eleazar son of Sira,” as reported.
Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II, who counted his reign from 170 BC; his thirty-eighth year is 132 BC. The translator arrived then and finished the work some time later.
Verse 5 is lacking in Swete's text and in the oldest Greek manuscripts; it belongs to the longer Greek recension (GII) and the Latin. So also verses 7 and 21 below.
GII adds: “Love of the Lord is glorious wisdom; to those to whom he appears he apportions her, so that they may see him.”
GII adds: “The fear of the Lord is a gift from the Lord, and it sets one upon paths of love.”
Or “he will be blessed”; the Greek manuscripts differ, as reported.
GII adds: “Both are gifts of God for peace; boasting opens wide for those who love him.”
The first line repeats 1:9; some editors treat it as a scribal repetition.
Greek “be justified.”
Or “before people”; the Hebrew is not extant here.

verses.text:
Child, if you come forward to serve the Lord,
get your soul ready for testing.

Keep your heart straight and stand firm,
and do not rush about in the time of calamity.

Cling to him and do not draw away,
so that you may be made great at your end.

Whatever is brought upon you, take it,
and in the turns of your humbling be patient.

For in fire gold is assayed,
and those acceptable to God in the furnace of humbling.{a}

Trust him, and he will take your part;
make your ways straight and set your hope on him.

You who fear the Lord, wait for his mercy,
and do not swerve, so that you do not fall.

You who fear the Lord, trust him,
and your wage will not slip away.

You who fear the Lord, hope for good things,
for gladness of the age and for mercy.{b}

Look at the generations of old and see:
who ever trusted the Lord and was shamed?
Who stayed in the fear of him and was abandoned?
Who called upon him and was overlooked by him?

For the Lord is full of pity and mercy;
he lets sins go and saves in a time of affliction.

Woe to timid hearts and drooping hands,
and to the sinner who sets foot on two tracks!

Woe to the drooping heart, for it has no trust!
Therefore it will have no shelter.

Woe to you who have thrown away your endurance!
What will you do on the day the Lord makes his visit?

Those who fear the Lord will not defy his words,
and those who love him will keep to his ways.

Those who fear the Lord will seek what pleases him,
and those who love him will be filled with the law.

Those who fear the Lord will make their hearts ready,
and before him they will bring their souls low.

notes.text: GII adds: “In sickness and in poverty be confident in him.”
GII adds: “For his reward is an everlasting gift with joy.”
Compare 2 Sam 24:14. Some witnesses add a line, as reported: “and as his name is, so also are his works.”

verses.text:
Listen to me, your father, children,
and act accordingly, so that you may be kept safe.

For the Lord gave the father glory over the children,
and made firm the mother's right over her sons.
Whoever honors a father atones for sins,
and whoever gives glory to his mother is like one storing up treasure.

Whoever honors a father will have gladness from his own children,
and on the day of his prayer he will be heard.

Whoever gives glory to a father will have long days,
and whoever heeds the Lord will give his mother rest;
he will serve his parents as a slave serves masters.{a}

In deed and in word honor your father,
so that blessing from him may come upon you.

For a father's blessing props up the houses of children,
but a mother's curse pulls up foundations.

Do not seek glory in your father's dishonor,
for that is no glory to you.

For a person's glory springs from his father's honor,
and a mother in disgrace is a reproach to her children.

Child, take your father's part in his old age,
and do not grieve him as long as he lives;

even if his understanding fails, bear with him,
and do not slight him while you are in your full strength.

For kindness to a father will not be forgotten;
it will be built up for you as a credit against sins;

Like one who reviles God is he who leaves his father in the lurch,
and one who stirs his mother to anger lies under the Lord's curse.

Child, carry out your tasks with mildness,
and you will be loved by those whom God accepts.{b}

The greater you are, the more you must make yourself low,
and you will find favor before the Lord.

[Many stand high and are famed,
yet to the gentle he discloses his secret things.]{c}

For the Lord's might is great,
and by the lowly he is glorified.

What is too hard for you, do not seek out;
what is too strong for you, do not search into.

Think about what you have been commanded,
for you have no need of things hidden.

Do not busy yourself with matters beyond your tasks,
for more than human understanding has already been shown you.

For their own conjecture has misled many,
and wicked fancies have made their thinking slide.

With no pupils in the eyes there will be no light;
and where knowledge is lacking, make no claim to wisdom.{d}

A stubborn heart will come to grief at the end,
and whoever loves danger will perish in it.

A stubborn heart will be weighed down by troubles,
and the sinner piles sin upon sin.

For the misfortune of the proud there is no cure,
since a plant of wickedness has taken root in him.

The mind of the prudent will ponder a parable,
and an attentive ear is what the wise desire.

Water puts out a blazing fire,
and almsgiving atones for sins.

Whoever repays favors keeps the future in mind,
and when he begins to fall he will find something to lean on.

notes.text: GII prefixes: “Whoever fears the Lord will honor his father.”
Greek “by an acceptable person”; the Hebrew (MS A, as reported) has “more than one who gives gifts.”
Verse 19 is lacking in Swete's text; it belongs to GII.
Verse 25 is lacking in Swete's text and in the main Greek manuscripts; it is found in other witnesses and in the Hebrew (MS A), as reported.

verses.text:
Child, do not cheat the poor man of his living,
and do not keep needy eyes waiting.

Do not pain a hungry soul,
and do not exasperate a man in his want.

Do not add turmoil to a heart already provoked,
and do not put off a gift to one in need.

Do not spurn a suppliant in distress,
and do not turn your face from a poor man.

Do not turn your eye from one who begs,
and give no one occasion to curse you;

for if he curses you in the bitterness of his soul,
his Maker will listen to his plea.

Make yourself dear to the assembly,
and bow your head to a great man.

Bend your ear to a poor man,
and answer him with peaceable words, mildly.

Rescue the wronged from the hand of the wrongdoer,
and do not lose heart when you sit in judgment.

Be like a father to orphans,
and like a husband to their mother;
then you will be like a son of the Most High,
and he will love you more than your own mother does.

Wisdom raises her sons on high
and takes hold of those who seek her.

Whoever loves her loves life,
and those who rise at dawn to meet her will be filled with gladness.

Whoever holds her fast will inherit glory,
and wherever she enters, the Lord gives blessing.

Those who wait on her minister to the Holy One,
and those who love her the Lord loves.

Whoever obeys her will judge nations,
and whoever attends to her will dwell in confidence.{a}

If he trusts her, he will inherit her,
and his descendants will hold her as a possession.

For at first she walks with him by twisting ways;
she brings fear and cowardice upon him
and torments him with her discipline
until she can trust his soul,
and she tests him with her ordinances.

Then she comes straight back to him again and gladdens him
and lays bare her secrets to him.

If he goes astray, she will abandon him
and hand him over to his own downfall.

Watch for the right time and guard yourself from evil,
and do not be ashamed where your own soul is concerned.

For there is a shame that leads to sin,
and there is a shame that is glory and grace.

Do not show favor to others against your own soul,
and do not let deference be your downfall.
Do not hold back a word when it can bring rescue.{b}

For by speech wisdom is made known,
and instruction by the utterance of the tongue.

Do not argue against the truth,
but be abashed at your own want of learning.

Feel no shame in owning up to your sins,
and do not push against the stream of a river.

Do not lay yourself down as a doormat for a fool,{c}
and do not show favor to a ruler.

Contend for the truth until death,
and the Lord God will fight on your side.

Do not be rough with your tongue,
or sluggish and slack in your works.

Do not be a lion in your own house,
or full of suspicious fancies among your servants.

Do not let your hand be held open to take
and clenched shut when it is time to pay back.

notes.text: The Hebrew (MS A), as reported, has “will judge truly” (one letter different from “nations”) and “will dwell in my inner rooms”; from verse 15 to 19 the Hebrew speaks in the first person as Wisdom.
GII adds: “and do not hide your wisdom for the sake of looking well.”
Greek “do not spread yourself beneath.”

verses.text:
Do not lean on your money,
and do not say, “I am self-sufficient.”

Do not follow your own soul and your strength
so as to walk in the cravings of your heart.

And do not say, “Who will lord it over me?”
for the Lord will surely exact punishment.

Do not say, “I sinned, and what happened to me?”
for the Lord is slow to anger.

Do not be so free of fear about atonement
that you add sin to sins.

Do not lean on unjust money,
for it will be no use to you on the day of disaster.

Stand fixed in what you understand,
and let your word be one.

Be quick to listen,
and give your answer with patience.

If you have understanding, answer your neighbor;
if not, put your hand on your mouth.

Glory and disgrace come by talking,
and a person's tongue can be his fall.
In great and small alike do not act in ignorance.

Do not lift yourself up in your soul's own counsel,
or your soul will be torn in pieces as by a bull;{a}

you will eat up your leaves and lose your fruit
and leave yourself like a dried-out tree.

A wicked soul ruins the one who owns it
and makes him a thing for his enemies to gloat over.

A sweet throat multiplies its friends,
and a gracious tongue multiplies friendly greetings.

Let those at peace with you be many,
but let your counselor be one in a thousand.

If you gain a friend, gain him by putting him to the test,
and do not be quick to trust him.

For there is a friend who is a friend when it suits him,
but will not stay by you on the day of your distress.

And there is a friend who changes into an enemy
and will lay bare the quarrel to your disgrace.

And there is a friend who shares your table
but will not stay by you on the day of your distress.

In your good times he will be like a second self
and speak freely to your servants;

if you are brought low, he will turn against you
and hide himself from your sight.

Keep yourself apart from your enemies,
and be on your guard with your friends.

A trustworthy friend is a stout covering;
the man who has found one has found treasure.

Nothing can be traded for a faithful friend,
and no scale can weigh his worth.

A faithful friend is a medicine that gives life,
and those who fear the Lord will find one.

Whoever fears the Lord keeps his friendship straight,
for as he is, so too is his neighbor.

Child, from your youth choose instruction,
and on into gray hairs you will keep finding wisdom.

How very rough she is to the untaught!
The witless will not stay with her.

Like a weighty stone for testing strength she will rest on him,
and he will lose no time in flinging her away.

For wisdom is as her name is,
and she is not plain to many.{b}

Listen, child, and accept my judgment,
and do not refuse my counsel.

Put your feet into her fetters
and your neck into her collar.

Set your shoulder under her and carry her,
and do not chafe at her bonds.

Come to her with all your soul,
and keep her ways with all your might.

Track her out and search, and she will become known to you;
and once you have hold of her, do not let her go.

For in the end you will discover her repose,
and she will turn for you into joy.

Her fetters will become a strong shelter for you,
and her collar a robe of glory.

For there is a golden ornament upon her,
and her bonds are a thread of violet.{c}

You will put her on like a robe of glory
and set her on yourself like a crown of exultation.

If you are willing, child, you will be trained,
and if you give your soul to it, you will be shrewd.

If you love to listen, you will take in,
and if you bend your ear, you will be wise.

Stand among the company of the elders;
who is wise? Fasten yourself to him.

Be eager to hear every godly discourse,
and do not let proverbs of understanding slip away from you.

If you see a man of understanding, get up early to go to him,
and let your foot wear down his doorsteps.

Ponder the ordinances of the Lord,
and meditate on his commandments at all times.
He himself will make your heart firm,
and the wisdom you long for will be given to you.

notes.text: The Greek is obscure; the Hebrew (MS A) differs, as reported.
Probably a play on Hebrew musar, “discipline,” which can also mean “withdrawn” or “held back.”
Greek hyakinthinos, the blue-violet dye of the tassels in Num 15:38.

verses.text: Do no evil, and evil will never lay hold of you.
Stand off from what is unjust, and it will swerve away from you.

Son, do not sow in the furrows of injustice,
and you will not reap it sevenfold.

Do not ask the Lord for high command,
or the king for a seat of honor.

Do not justify yourself before the Lord,
and do not play the sage in the king's presence.

Do not seek to become a judge,
or you may not be strong enough to root out injustice;
you may be overawed in the presence of a powerful man
and lay a stumbling block in the path of your uprightness.

Do not sin against the populace of the city,
and do not throw yourself down in the crowd.

Do not tie on a sin twice over,
for not even for one will you go unpunished.

Do not say, “He will regard the abundance of my gifts,
and when I bring them to God Most High, he will take them.”

Do not lose heart in your prayer,
and do not neglect to give alms.

Do not laugh at a person in bitterness of soul,
for there is One who brings low and lifts up.

Do not plow up a lie against your brother,
or do the like to a friend.

Refuse to tell any lie at all,
for the habit of it leads to no good.

Do not prattle in the company of elders,
and do not repeat yourself in your prayer.

Do not hate laborious work,
or farming, which was created by the Most High.

Do not reckon yourself in the throng of sinners;
bear in mind that wrath does not linger.

Humble your soul to the utmost,
for the punishment of the ungodly is fire and worms.{a}

Do not trade a friend for something of no account,
or a true brother for the gold of Ophir.{b}

Do not pass over a wise and good wife,
for her grace is worth more than gold.

Do not ill-treat a servant who works in good faith,
or a hired man who gives himself to the work.

Let your soul love a good servant;
do not deprive him of his freedom.{c}

Do you have cattle? Look after them;
and if they are useful to you, keep them.

Do you have children? Train them,
and bend their necks from their youth.

Do you have daughters? Take care of their bodies,
and do not let your face shine on them too brightly.

Give a daughter in marriage, and you will have finished a great work;
but give her to a man of understanding.

Is there a wife to your liking? Do not send her away;
but to a wife you loathe do not entrust yourself.{d}

With your whole heart give glory to your father,
and do not forget the birth pangs of your mother.

Remember that through them you came into being;
and what can you repay them for what they gave you?

With all your soul hold the Lord in awe,
and hold his priests in high regard.

With all your strength love the One who made you,
and do not abandon his ministers.

Fear the Lord and give glory to the priest,
and give him his portion as you were commanded:
the firstfruits and the guilt offering, the gift of the shoulders,
the sacrifice of sanctification, and the firstfruits of holy things.{e}

Stretch out your hand to the poor as well,
so that your blessing may be made complete.

A gift brings grace before everyone who lives;
do not withhold kindness even from the dead.

Do not keep away from those who weep,
but mourn with those who mourn.

Do not be slow to visit the sick,
for by such deeds you will be loved.

In all you say, remember your last end,
and you will never sin.

notes.text: The Hebrew (MS A), as reported, reads “for what awaits mortals is worms”; the Greek introduces the idea of punishment by fire (compare Isa 66:24).
Greek Soupheir, the gold-land of Ophir.
Compare Exod 21:2; Deut 15:12–18.
The second line is lacking in Swete's text; it is found in other witnesses and in the Hebrew (MS A), as reported.
Compare Lev 7:28–36; Num 18:8–20; Deut 18:3–4.

verses.text:
Do not fight it out with a powerful man,
or you may fall into his hands.

Do not quarrel with a rich man,
or he may set his weight against you;
for gold has ruined many
and has bent the hearts of kings.

Do not fight it out with a loud-mouthed man,
and do not pile wood on his fire.

Do not make sport with an ill-bred man,
or your forebears may be insulted.

Do not reproach a person who is turning from sin;
remember that we all are liable to penalty.

Do not dishonor a person in his old age,
for some of us also are growing old.

Do not gloat over the dead;
remember that we all come to our end.

Do not disregard the discourse of the wise,
but occupy yourself with their proverbs;
for from them you will learn instruction
and how to serve the great.

Do not miss the talk of the aged,
for they too learned from their fathers;
from them you will learn understanding
and how to give an answer when it is needed.

Do not kindle a sinner's coals,
or you may be scorched in the flame of his fire.

Do not jump up and leave before an insolent man,
or he will sit like an ambush at your mouth.

Do not lend to a man stronger than you;
and if you lend, count it as lost.

Do not stand surety beyond your means;
and if you do, give thought to paying.

Do not go to law against a judge,
for they will decide for him as his rank requires.

Do not take to the road beside a daredevil,
or he will be heavy on you;
he will act on his own whim,
and his folly will drag you down to ruin with him.

Do not take counsel with a fool,
for he cannot keep a matter to himself.

Do nothing secret in front of a stranger,
for you do not know what it will bring forth.

Do not lay your heart open to everyone,
and do not let anyone count it a favor to you.{a}

notes.text: Or, by another reading, “and do not drive away your good fortune”; the Greek is uncertain.

verses.text:
Do not be jealous over the wife you hold close,
and do not school her in evil to your own hurt.

Do not give your soul to a woman
so that she sets her foot upon your strength.

Do not go to meet a loose woman,
or you may fall into her snares.

Do not linger with a woman who sings to the harp,
or you may be caught by her tricks.

Do not fix your gaze on a maiden,
or you may be tripped up and pay fines because of her.{a}

Do not give your soul to prostitutes,
or you may lose your inheritance.

Do not peer about in the lanes of the city,
and do not wander in its deserted corners.

Turn your eye away from a shapely woman,
and do not stare at beauty that belongs to another;
by a woman's beauty many have been led astray,
and from it desire is kindled like fire.

Never sit at table with a married woman,
and do not carouse with her over wine,
or your soul may lean toward her,
and in your passion you may slide into ruin.{b}

Do not desert an old friend,
for a new one does not match him.
A new friend is new wine;
when it has grown old, you will drink it with gladness.

Do not envy a sinner's glory,
for you do not know how he will be overthrown.

Do not delight in what delights the ungodly;
remember that they will not go unpunished before they reach Hades.

As far as you can, size up your neighbors,
and consult with the wise.

Let your discussion be with people of understanding,
and let all your talk be about the law of the Most High.

Let righteous men be your companions at table,
and let your boasting be in the fear of the Lord.

A work wins praise for the craftsman's hand,
and a ruler of the people for the wisdom of his speech.

A man of loose tongue is dreaded in his city,
and one who is rash in his talk will be hated.

notes.text: Compare Exod 22:16–17; Deut 22:28–29.
Greek “with your spirit”; the Hebrew (MS A), as reported, has “in blood,” that is, to a death sentence (compare Lev 20:10).

verses.text:
A wise judge will school his people,
and the rule of a man of understanding will be well ordered.

As the people's judge is, so are his officers,
and as the city's ruler is, so are all who dwell in it.

An unschooled king will ruin his people,
but a city is settled through the good sense of those in power.

Authority over the earth lies in the Lord's hand,
and at the right season he will raise up over it the one who is fit.

A man's success lies in the Lord's hand,
and on the person of the scribe he will lay his own glory.{a}

Do not nurse rage at your neighbor for every wrong,
and do nothing by deeds of insolence.

Arrogance is hateful before the Lord and before people,
and injustice gives offense to both.

Kingship is shifted from nation to nation
because of injustice and insolence and money.{b}

Why is earth and ashes proud?
Even while alive, its innards are cast away.{c}

A long illness — the physician scoffs at it;
a king today, and tomorrow he will be dead.

For when a person dies,
creeping things and wild beasts and worms are what he inherits.

The start of human pride is standing off from the Lord:
the heart has withdrawn from its Maker.

For the start of pride is sin,
and whoever clings to it showers forth abomination.
On this account the Lord brought on them strange calamities
and overturned them utterly.

The Lord has pulled down the thrones of rulers
and seated the gentle in their stead.

The Lord has plucked up the roots of nations
and planted the lowly in their stead.

The Lord has overturned the lands of nations
and destroyed them down to the foundations of the earth.

Some of them he has dried up and destroyed,
and he has made their remembrance cease from the earth.

Arrogance was not created for human beings,
nor savage anger for those born of women.

What seed is held in honor? Human seed.
What seed is held in honor? Those who fear the Lord.
What seed is held in dishonor? Human seed.
What seed is held in dishonor? Those who step over commandments.

Among brothers their leader is held in honor,
and those who fear the Lord are so in his eyes.

[The fear of the Lord is where acceptance begins,
but hardness and arrogance are where rejection begins.]{d}

Rich man, man of note, and poor man alike —
their boast is the fear of the Lord.

It is not just to dishonor a poor man who has understanding,
and it is not proper to give glory to a sinful man.

Magnate, judge, and ruler will receive honor,
yet not one of them stands above the man who fears the Lord.

Free men will wait upon a wise servant,
and a man of knowledge will not grumble at it.

Do not play the sage over doing your work,
and do not give yourself airs in the time of your want.

Better the man who works and has plenty of all things
than the one who struts about with airs and lacks bread.

Child, give your soul glory in meekness,
and give it honor according to its worth.

Who will declare righteous one who sins against his own soul?
And who will give glory to one who dishonors his own life?

A poor man is given glory for his knowledge,
and a rich man is given glory for his riches.

One given glory in poverty — how much more in riches!
And one held in dishonor in riches — how much more in poverty!

notes.text: Greek grammateus, “scribe”; the Hebrew (MS A), as reported, has “ruler” or “lawgiver” (mehoqeq).
GII adds: “Nothing is more lawless than one who loves money, for such a one puts his own soul up for sale.”
The Greek is difficult (literally “I cast away”); the sense is that the body is decaying even in life.
Verse 21 is lacking in Swete's text; it belongs to the longer Greek recension (GII).

verses.text:
The wisdom of a lowly man will lift up his head
and seat him in the midst of great men.

Do not praise a man for his good looks,
and do not loathe a person for how he appears.

Small among winged things is the bee,
but its fruit is first among sweet things.

Many tyrants have sat down upon the ground,
and one no one suspected has worn the diadem.

Many potentates have been deeply disgraced,
and men of note have been handed into others' hands.

Before you examine, find no fault;
understand first, and then rebuke.

Before you hear, do not answer,
and do not throw in words in the middle of another's speech.

Do not wrangle over a matter that is no need of yours,
and do not sit in session when sinners give judgment.

There is one who labors and toils and hurries,
and he falls all the further behind.

There is one who is sluggish and in want of help,
short of strength and rich in poverty;
and the eyes of the Lord have looked on him for good,
and he has set him upright out of his low estate

and lifted up his head,
and many have been astonished at him.

Good things and bad, life and death,
poverty and riches — they come from the Lord.

[From the Lord come wisdom, discernment, and knowing the law;
from him come love and the paths of good deeds.]{a}

[Wandering and darkness were formed along with sinners,
and for those who glory in wickedness, evil ages with them.]

The Lord's gift abides with the godly,
and his good pleasure will prosper them to the age.

There is one who grows rich by vigilance and pinching,
and this is the share of his wage:

when he says, “I have found rest,
and now I will eat from my goods,”
he does not know what time will go by
before he leaves them to others and dies.

Stand fast in your covenant and be occupied with it,
and grow old in your work.

The blessing of the Lord is in the wage of the godly,
and in a swift hour he makes his blessing burst into bloom.

Do not say, “What need have I,
and what good things will be mine from now on?”

Do not say, “I am self-sufficient,
and what evil can be mine from now on?”

On a day of good things, bad things slip from memory,
and on a day of bad things, good things are not recalled.

For it is a light thing for the Lord on the day of one's end
to pay a person back according to his ways.

An hour of hardship makes delight forgotten,
and at a person's end his deeds are uncovered.

Count no one blessed before his end;
by his children a man will be known.

Do not bring every man into your house,
for the snares of the treacherous are many.

A decoy partridge in a basket — such is the heart of the proud,
and like a spy he watches for your fall;

for he lies in ambush, turning good things to evil,
and on things worth choosing he will fix a blemish.

From one spark of fire a whole hearth of coals grows,
and a sinful man lies in ambush for blood.

Beware of a wrongdoer, for he devises wickedness,
or he may give you a blemish to the age.

Lodge a stranger in your house, and he will twist you round with troubles
and make you a stranger to your own.

notes.text: Verses 15 and 16 are lacking in Swete's text; they belong to the longer Greek recension (GII).

verses.text:
If you do good, know whom you are doing it for,
and there will be thanks for your good deeds.

Do good to a godly man, and you will find repayment,
if not from him, then from the Most High.

No good things come to one who persists in evil,
or to one who gives no alms.

Give to the godly man,
and do not take the sinner's part.

For the Most High himself hates sinners
and will pay out vengeance on the ungodly.

Give to the good man,
and do not take the sinner's part.

A friend is not made known{a} in good times,
and an enemy is not hidden in bad times.

In a man's good times his enemies are in sorrow,
and in his bad times even his friend goes off from him.

Never trust your enemy,
for as bronze corrodes, so does his wickedness.

Even if he humbles himself and walks about stooped,
set your soul on watch and guard yourself from him,
and be to him like one who has wiped a mirror clean,
and you will know that it has not rusted through to the end.{b}

Do not stand him next to you,
or he may overturn you and take your place;
do not seat him at your right hand,
or he may go after your seat,
and at the last you will recognize my words
and be pierced by what I have said.

Who has pity on a charmer bitten by his serpent,
or on anyone who comes close to wild animals?

So too with one who goes about with a sinful man
and is mixed up in his sins.

He will stay with you an hour,
but if you lean aside, he will not hold out.

With his lips the enemy will speak sweetly,
but in his heart he will plot to tip you into a pit;
with his eyes the enemy will shed tears,
but if he finds his moment, he will not be sated with blood.

If evils meet you, you will find him there before you,
and as though helping, he will clip your heel.

He will wag his head and clap his hands
and whisper much and change his countenance.

notes.text: Greek “will not be punished”; probably a scribal slip for “will not be known,” which the Hebrew supports, as reported.
Ancient mirrors were polished bronze, which tarnished and had to be wiped.

verses.text:
Whoever touches pitch will be smeared,
and whoever goes about with an arrogant man will become like him.

Do not lift a load too heavy for you,
and do not go about with one stronger and richer than you.
What partnership can the clay pot have with the kettle?
This one will knock against it, and that one will be smashed.

A rich man does wrong, and he even snorts with anger;
a poor man is wronged, and he must also plead.

If you are of use, he will work you;
and if you fall short, he will abandon you.

If you have means, he will live with you
and empty you out, and it will cost him no pain.

He will shame you with his dainties
until he has emptied you out two or three times,
and at the last he will make sport of you.
After this he will see you and abandon you
and wag his head at you.

Take care not to be led astray
and humbled in your merriment.{a}

When a potentate calls you in, keep your distance,
and he will call you in all the more.

Do not crowd in, or you may be thrust away;
and do not stand far off, or you may be forgotten.

Pitiless is the one who does not keep words to himself;
he will not spare you harm and chains.

Keep watch and take great heed,
for you are walking side by side with your own fall.

Every living creature loves its like,
and every person loves his neighbor.

All flesh flocks together by kind,
and a man will cleave to the one who is like him.

What partnership can a wolf have with a lamb?
So it is with a sinner toward a godly man.

What peace has a hyena with a dog?
And what peace has a rich man with a poor one?

Wild asses in the desert are the quarry of lions;
just so, the poor are the grazing ground of the rich.

Lowliness is an abomination to the proud;
just so, a poor man is an abomination to the rich.

When a rich man totters, he is propped up by friends,
but when a lowly man falls, he is shoved away by friends too.

A rich man speaks, and all go quiet,
and they lift his word up to the clouds.
A poor man speaks, and they say, “Who is this?”
and if he stumbles, they help to knock him down.

Riches are good where there is no sin,
and poverty is evil, in the mouth of the ungodly.

A person's heart alters his face,
whether for good or for evil.

The trace of a heart in good things is a cheerful face,
but the finding out of proverbs is reasoning with toil.

notes.text: The Hebrew (MS A), as reported, has “in your folly.”
Verse 14 is lacking in Swete's text; it belongs to the longer Greek recension (GII).

verses.text:
Blessed is the man who has not slipped with his mouth
and has not been pierced with grief for sin.

Blessed is the one whose soul has not condemned him
and who has not fallen from his hope.

Riches are not fitting for a stingy man,
and to a begrudging person, what good is money?

One who gathers by stinting his own soul gathers for others,
and on his good things others will live in luxury.

One who is mean to himself — to whom will he be good?
He will take no joy in his own money.

No one is meaner than the man who begrudges himself,
and this is the repayment of his wickedness.

Even if he does good, he does it by forgetfulness,
and at the last he lays bare his wickedness.

Evil is the one who begrudges with his eye,
turning away his face and overlooking souls.

The eye of the greedy is not filled by his share,
and wicked injustice dries up the soul.

An evil eye is grudging over bread,
and at his own table it is lacking.

Child, as far as you have the means, treat yourself well,
and bring offerings to the Lord worthily.

Remember that death will not delay,
and the covenant of Hades has not been shown to you.

Before you come to your end, do good to a friend,
and as far as your strength allows, reach out and give to him.

Do not cheat yourself of a good day,
and do not let a share of good desire slip past you.

Will you not leave your labors to another,
and your toils for dividing by lot?

Give and take, and treat your soul kindly,
for in Hades there is no seeking of delight.

All flesh grows old like a garment,
for the covenant from the age is, “You shall surely die.”

Like leaves flourishing on a thick tree,
some it drops and others it puts forth:
so is the generation of flesh and blood,
one comes to its end and another is born.

Every work decays and gives out,
and the one who works at it will go away along with it.

Blessed is the man who will meditate on wisdom
and who will reason with his understanding,

who ponders her ways in his heart
and will gain insight into her secrets.

Go out after her like a tracker,
and lie in wait at her entryways.

He peeps in through her windows
and will listen at her doorways;

he lodges close beside her house
and will drive a peg into her walls;

he will pitch his tent at her side
and will lodge in a lodging of good things;

he will set his children in her shelter
and will camp beneath her branches;

Under her he will find cover from the burning heat,
and in her splendor he will lodge.

The one who fears the Lord will do this,
and the one who holds fast to the law will lay hold of her.

Like a mother she will come out to meet him,
and as a bride taken in her youth she will receive him.

She will feed him the bread of understanding
and give him the water of wisdom to drink.

He will lean on her and not be bent,
and he will hold to her and not be put to shame.

She will lift him up above his neighbors
and open his mouth in the midst of the assembly.

Gladness and a crown of exultation
and an everlasting name will be his inheritance.

Senseless people will never lay hold of her,
and sinful men will never see her.

She is far from arrogance,
and lying men will never call her to mind.

Praise is not seemly in a sinner's mouth,
for it was not sent from the Lord.

For praise will be spoken in wisdom,
and the Lord will prosper it.

Do not say, “It was through the Lord that I fell away,”
for what he hates, you are not to do.

Do not say, “He is the one who led me astray,”
for he has no need of a sinful man.

Every abomination the Lord has hated,
and it is not dear to those who fear him.

He himself made humankind from the beginning
and left them in the hand of their own counsel.{a}

If you choose, you will keep the commandments,
and acting in good faith is a matter of your own choosing.

He has laid before you fire and water;
stretch out your hand to whichever you choose.

Before human beings lie life and death,
and whichever one pleases him will be given to him.

For great is the wisdom of the Lord;
he is strong in dominion and beholds all things;

and his eyes are upon those who fear him,
and he himself will take note of every human deed.

He has commanded no one to be ungodly,
and he has given no one leave to sin.

notes.text: Greek diaboulion, “deliberation”; the Hebrew, as reported, has yetser, “inclination,” the word from which later Jewish teaching on the good and evil inclinations developed.

verses.text:
Do not long for a crowd of useless children,
and do not take delight in ungodly sons.

If they multiply, do not delight in them,
unless the fear of the Lord is with them.

For through one man of understanding a city will be peopled,
but a tribe of the lawless will be laid waste.

Many such things my eyes have seen,
and my ear has heard things mightier than these.

In a gathering of sinners a fire will be kindled,
and in a disobedient nation wrath has blazed up.

He did not make atonement for the giants of old,{b}
who revolted in their strength.

He did not spare those among whom Lot sojourned,
whom he abhorred for their arrogance.

He did not pity the nation marked for destruction,{c}
those driven out in their sins;

so too with the six hundred thousand foot soldiers
who banded together in their hardness of heart.{d}

As great as his mercy, so great also is his reproof;
he will judge a man according to his works.

The sinner will not escape with his plunder,
and the endurance of the godly will not be cut short.

He will make room for every act of mercy;
each will find according to his works.

[The Lord made Pharaoh hard, so that he would not acknowledge him,
that his deeds might be known throughout the world below heaven.]{e}

[His mercy is plain to all his creation,
and he apportioned his light and his darkness to Adam.]

Do not say, “I will hide myself from the Lord,
and who from on high will remember me?
Among a greater people I will not be remembered;
for what is my soul in a creation beyond measure?

Look: heaven and the heaven of heaven,
the abyss and the earth, will shake when he visits.

The mountains along with the foundations of the earth,
when he looks on them, are shaken with trembling.

Yet no heart will give thought to these things,
and who will ponder his ways?

As a squall that no person will see,
so the greater part of his works are hidden.

Works of justice — who will announce them?
Or who will wait for them? For the covenant is far off.”

Lacking in heart is the one who ponders these things,
and a senseless man who has gone astray ponders folly.

Listen to me, child, and learn knowledge,
and set your heart on my words.

I will reveal instruction by weight
and announce knowledge with exactness.

When the Lord judged his works from the beginning,
and from their making he marked out their portions,

he set his works in array to the age,
and their first principles for their generations;
they neither hunger nor grow weary,
and they do not give out from their works.

Not one of them jostles its neighbor,
and to the age they will not disobey his word.

And after this the Lord looked down on the earth
and filled it with his good things.

With every kind of living soul he covered its face,
and to it they return.

notes.text: Greek “their place,” perhaps meaning their standing or number; GII and the Hebrew add lines here, as reported.
The Canaanites (compare Deut 7:1–2; 20:16–18).
Israel in the wilderness (Num 11:21; 14:22–35).
Verses 15 and 16 are lacking in Swete's text; they belong to the longer Greek recension (GII). Compare Exod 7–11.

verses.text:
The Lord formed a human being from the earth
and sent him back into it again.

Days by number and a set span he gave them,
and he gave them authority over the things on it.

He clothed them with strength befitting himself{a}
and made them after his own image.

He laid the dread of them on all flesh,
to be lords over beasts and birds.

Deliberation and tongue and eyes,
ears and a heart to think with, he gave them.

With knowing and discerning he filled them,
and he pointed out to them good and evil.

He set his eye on their hearts
to show them the greatness of his works,{c}
so that they would recount the greatness of his works,{d}
and they will praise the name of his holiness.

He set knowledge before them
and gave them the law of life as their allotment.

An everlasting covenant he established with them
and pointed out his judgments to them.

Their eyes saw the greatness of his glory,
and their ear heard the glory of his voice.

He said to them, “Keep away from everything unjust,”
and he gave each of them commands about his neighbor.

Their ways are before him at all times;
they will not be hidden from his eyes.

[Their ways from youth lean toward evil,
and they cannot make themselves hearts of flesh in place of stone.]

For each nation he appointed a ruler,
but Israel is the Lord's own portion.{e}

[Israel, his firstborn, he rears with discipline,
and sharing with him the light of his love, he does not neglect him.]

All their works are as plain to him as the sun,
and his eyes are always on their ways.

Their injustices are not hidden from him,
and all their sins are before the Lord.

[But the Lord, being good and knowing what they are made of,
has not left or forsaken them, but has spared them.]

A man's almsgiving is like a signet with him,
and a person's kindness he will keep like the pupil of the eye.

Afterward he will rise up and repay them
and render their due on their own heads.

Yet for those who repent he has granted a way back,
and he comforts those whose endurance is giving out.

Turn back to the Lord and leave off sins;
beg before his face and make the stumbling less.

Return to the Most High and turn away from injustice,
and hate abomination with all your might.

Who will praise the Most High in Hades,
in place of the living who give him thanks?

From a dead man, as from one who is not, thanksgiving perishes;
the living and healthy will praise the Lord.

How great the mercy of the Lord,
and his atonement for those who turn to him!

For not all things can be in human beings,
since a son of man is not deathless.

What is brighter than the sun? Yet even it fails.
And flesh and blood will ponder evil.

He inspects the host of the height of heaven,
but human beings are all earth and ashes.

notes.text: Greek “according to themselves”; the Latin and Syriac point to “like himself.”
Verse 5 is lacking in Swete's text; it belongs to the longer Greek recension (GII), which counts the five senses as powers given by the Lord. So also verses 16, 18, and 21 below.
GII adds: “and he granted them to boast of his wonders to the age.”
Swete's text, like the NRSV, has verses 9 and 10 in the reverse order; they are given here in numerical order.
Compare Deut 32:8–9 in the Greek, where the nations are allotted “according to the number of the angels of God.”

verses.text: The one who lives to the age created all things alike;{a}
the Lord alone will be declared righteous.

To no one has he given leave to declare his works;
and who will track out his mighty acts?

The strength of his greatness — who will count it up?
And who will go on to tell out his mercies?

One cannot take away or add,
and one cannot track out the wonders of the Lord.

When a person has finished, then he is beginning,
and when he leaves off, then he will be at a loss.

What is a human being, and what is he good for?
What is his good, and what is his evil?
The number of a man's days — a hundred years is many.{c}

Like a drop of water from the sea and a pebble of sand,
so are a few years set in the day of the age.

That is why the Lord bears long with them
and lavishes his mercy upon them.

He saw and recognized that their overthrow is wretched;
therefore he made his atonement abundant.

A person's mercy is toward his neighbor,
but the Lord's mercy is toward all flesh;
he reproves and trains and teaches
and turns them back, as a shepherd his flock.

He has mercy on those who welcome discipline
and who hurry toward his judgments.

Child, do not attach blame to good deeds,
or the grief of words to any gift.

Will the dew not cool the burning wind?
Just so, a word is better than a gift.

See — is not a word above a good gift?
And both are found with a gracious man.

A fool reproaches without grace,
and a begrudging man's gift makes the eyes waste away.

Before you speak, learn,
and before sickness, look after yourself.

Before judgment, examine yourself,
and in the hour of visitation you will find atonement.

Before you fall ill, humble yourself,
and in the season of sins, show a turning back.

Let nothing keep you from paying a vow in its season,
and do not wait until death to be set right.

Before you vow, make yourself ready,
and do not be like a man who puts the Lord to the test.

Remember the wrath of the end days
and the season of vengeance, when he turns away his face.

Remember the time of hunger in the time of fullness,
poverty and want in days of riches.

From dawn until dusk the season shifts,
and all things are quick before the Lord.

A wise man will be wary in everything,
and in days of sinning he will guard against offense.

Every man of understanding knows wisdom,
and to the one who finds her he will give acknowledgment.

Those with understanding in sayings have themselves become wise
and have poured out apt proverbs.

Do not walk behind your desires,
and keep yourself back from your cravings.

If you grant your soul the good pleasure of desire,
it will make you a thing for your enemies to gloat over.

Do not take delight in much luxury,
and do not be bound to its outlay.

Do not become a beggar by feasting on borrowed money
when you have nothing in your purse.{d}

notes.text: Greek koinē, “in common,” “alike”; the Latin reads “all at once.”
Verse 3 is lacking in Swete's text; it belongs to the longer Greek recension (GII).
GII adds: “but no one can reckon the sleep of each one in eternity.”
GII adds: “for you will be plotting against your own life.”

verses.text:
A laborer who is a drunkard will not grow rich;
one who scorns small things will fall little by little.

Wine and women make men of understanding fall away,
and one who cleaves to prostitutes grows more brazen.

Rot and worms will inherit him,
and a brazen soul will be taken off.

One who trusts quickly is light of heart,
and one who sins will offend against his own soul.
One who takes delight in his heart will be condemned,{a}
and one who hates chatter has less of evil.

Never repeat a word,
and you will be none the worse.

To friend or to foe do not tell it,
and unless it is a sin for you, do not uncover it;

for he has heard you and kept watch on you,
and in due season he will hate you.

Have you heard a word? Let it die with you.
Take heart; it will not burst you.

Over a word a fool goes into labor,
like a woman in labor over her infant.

An arrow fixed in the flesh of the thigh —
so is a word in a fool's belly.

Reprove a friend: perhaps he did not do it;
and if he did something, so that he does not add to it.

Reprove a neighbor: perhaps he did not say it;
and if he has said it, so that he does not say it again.

Reprove a friend, for it is often slander,
and do not believe every word.

There is one who slips, but not from the soul;
and who has not offended with his tongue?

Reprove your neighbor before you threaten,
and give place to the law of the Most High.

[The fear of the Lord is where acceptance begins,
and wisdom wins his love.]{b}

[Knowing the Lord's commandments is a discipline that gives life,
and those who do what pleases him pluck the fruit of the tree of deathlessness.]

The whole of wisdom is the fear of the Lord,
and every wisdom includes carrying out the law.

[When a slave tells his master, “I will not do as you please,”
even if he does it afterward, he angers the one who feeds him.]

Knowing evil is not wisdom,
and where sinners counsel there is no good sense.

There is a craftiness, and it is an abomination,
and there is a fool who merely lacks wisdom.

Better one who falls short in understanding and is God-fearing
than one who abounds in good sense and steps over the law.

There is a cleverness that is exact and unjust,
and there is one who twists a favor to bring a judgment to light.

There is a wicked man who goes bent over in black,
and his insides are full of deceit;

he lowers his face and plays deaf,
but where he is not noticed he will get the jump on you;

and if for lack of strength he is kept from sinning,
when he finds the season he will do harm.

From his look a man is known,
and from meeting his face a man of understanding is known.

A man's dress and the grin of his teeth
and the steps he takes report what he is.

notes.text: GII adds: “but one who resists pleasures crowns his life.” Verse 5b and part of verse 6 in older English versions also come from GII.
Verses 18, 19, and 21 are lacking in Swete's text; they belong to the longer Greek recension (GII).

verses.text:
There is a reproof that is out of season,
and there is one who keeps silent, and he is shrewd.
How much better to reprove than to nurse anger!
And one who confesses will be kept from loss.

A eunuch's lust to deflower a girl —
such is one who works out judgments by force.

There is one who keeps silent and is found wise,
and there is one who is hated for great chatter.

There is one who keeps silent, for he has no answer,
and there is one who keeps silent, knowing the season.

A wise man will hold his peace until the season,
but a boaster and a fool will overshoot the season.

One who multiplies words will be loathed,
and one who takes power to himself will be hated.

There is good luck for a man in bad things,
and there is a windfall that turns to loss.

There is a gift that will not profit you,
and there is a gift whose repayment is double.

There is a loss on account of glory,
and there is one who has raised his head from low estate.

There is one who buys much for little
and pays for it sevenfold.

The wise in speech makes himself loved,
but the graces of fools will be poured out for nothing.

A senseless man's gift will not profit you,
for his eyes are many instead of one.{a}
How often, and by how many, will he be laughed to scorn!

A slip on the pavement is better than one with the tongue;
so the fall of the wicked will come swiftly.

A graceless man is a tale told out of season;
it will be always in the mouth of the unschooled.

A proverb from a fool's mouth will be refused,
for he will not say it in its season.

There is one who is kept from sinning by want,
and at his rest he will not be pricked.

There is one who ruins his soul through shame
and ruins it before a senseless face.

There is one who from shame makes promises to a friend
and has gained him as an enemy for nothing.

A lie is a foul blemish on a man;
it will be always in the mouth of the unschooled.

A thief is preferable to one who lies constantly,
but both of them will inherit ruin.

The way of a liar is dishonor,
and his shame is with him always.

One wise in sayings will advance himself,
and a shrewd man will please the great.

One who works the ground will heap his threshing floor high,
and one who pleases the great will atone for injustice.

Presents and gifts blind the eyes of the wise,
and like a muzzle on the mouth they turn reproofs aside.

Wisdom hidden and treasure out of sight —
what profit is in either?

Better a man who hides his folly
than a man who hides his wisdom.

notes.text: That is, he looks for much in return.

verses.text:
Child, have you sinned? Do it no more,
and make supplication about your former sins.

All lawlessness is like a two-edged sword;
its wound has no healing.

Panic and insolence will lay waste riches;
so the house of the proud will be laid waste.

A poor man's supplication goes from his mouth to his ears,{a}
and his judgment comes in haste.

One who hates reproof walks in the sinner's track,
but one who fears the Lord will turn back in his heart.

The mighty in tongue is known from far off,
but the man of understanding knows when he slips.

One who builds his house with other people's money
is like one gathering stones for his own grave mound.{b}

Tow heaped together is a gathering of the lawless,
and their end is a flame of fire.

The road of sinners is smoothed with paving stones,
and at its end is the pit of Hades.

One who keeps the law masters its intent,
and the completion of the fear of the Lord is wisdom.

One who is not clever will not be schooled,
but there is a cleverness that multiplies bitterness.

A wise man's knowledge will swell like a flood,
and his counsel like a spring of life.

A fool's insides are like a broken jar;
he will hold no knowledge.

If a knowing man hears a wise word,
he will praise it and add to it;
the self-indulgent man heard it, and it displeased him,
and he cast it away behind his back.

A fool's narration is like a load on the road,
but on the lips of the understanding grace will be found.

The mouth of the shrewd will be sought in the assembly,
and they will ponder his words in their hearts.

Like a house laid waste, so is wisdom to a fool,
and the knowledge of the witless is talk no one can test.

Fetters on the feet is discipline to the senseless,
and like manacles on the right hand.

A fool lifts up his voice in laughter,
but a clever man will scarcely smile, and quietly.

Like a golden ornament is discipline to the shrewd,
and like a bracelet on the right arm.

A fool's foot is quick into a house,
but a man of experience is abashed before a face.

A senseless man peeps from the door into a house,
but a well-schooled man will stand outside.

It is bad schooling for a man to listen at a door;
the shrewd man would be weighed down with the dishonor.

The lips of strangers will be heavy with these things,{c}
but the words of the understanding are weighed on the scale.

In fools' mouths is their heart,
but in the heart of the wise is their mouth.

When the ungodly man curses Satan,
he curses his own soul.{d}

The whisperer stains his own soul
and will be hated in his neighborhood.

notes.text: That is, to God's ears.
So some witnesses (chōma); others read “for winter” (cheimōna).
The Greek of the first line is uncertain; some witnesses read “the lips of the talkative.”
Greek satanas, “the adversary”; the sense may be that the wicked, in cursing his opponent, calls the curse down on himself.

verses.text:
A filthy stone — that is what the idler is like,
and everyone will hiss at his disgrace.

A lump of dung — that is what the idler is like;
everyone who picks it up will shake off his hand.

Shame for a father is an unschooled son,
and a daughter is born to his loss.

A shrewd daughter will inherit a husband of her own,
but she who brings shame is a grief to the one who sired her.

A brazen daughter shames father and husband,
and by both she will be held in dishonor.

Like music in mourning is a tale out of season,
but whips and discipline are wisdom in every season.

[Children brought up to a good life
cover the humble birth of their parents.]{a}

[Children who swell with contempt and coarseness from lack of training
stain the noble birth of their kin.]

One who teaches a fool is gluing a potsherd,
rousing a sleeper out of deep sleep.

One who narrates to a fool narrates to a man who is nodding off,
and at the end he will say, “What is it?”

Weep over a dead man, for light has failed him,
and weep over a fool, for understanding has failed him;
weep more gently over a dead man, for he has gone to rest,
but the fool's life is worse than death.

For the dead, mourning lasts seven days;
for the fool and the ungodly, every day he lives.

What will be heavier than lead?
And what is its name but “Fool”?

Sand and salt and a lump of iron
are easier to carry than a man without understanding.

Wooden binding fastened into a building
will not be loosed by a quake;
just so, a heart fixed on considered counsel
will not cower at the critical moment.

A heart set firm on thoughts of understanding
is like plaster ornament on a smooth wall.

One who pricks an eye will bring down tears,
and one who pricks a heart brings its feeling to light.

One who throws a stone at birds scares them off,
and one who reviles a friend will dissolve the friendship.

Even if you have drawn a sword on a friend,
do not despair, for there can be a way back.

If you have opened your mouth against a friend,
do not be anxious, for there can be reconciliation —
except for reproach and arrogance, the uncovering of a secret, and a treacherous blow;
at these any friend will run away.

Gain trust with your neighbor in his poverty,
so that in his good things you may be filled together;
stay by him in the season of his affliction,
so that you may share in his inheritance together.

Ahead of fire comes the steam of a furnace and smoke;
just so, abuse comes ahead of bloodshed.

I will not be ashamed to shelter a friend,
and from his face I will not hide.

And if evil happens to me through him,
everyone who hears will be on guard against him.

Who will set a guard upon my mouth
and a seal of shrewdness upon my lips,
so that I do not fall by them
and my tongue does not destroy me?

notes.text: Verses 7 and 8 are lacking in Swete's text; they belong to the longer Greek recension (GII).
Greek charakes, “stakes”; some witnesses read “pebbles.”

verses.text:
Who will set whips over my thinking
and wisdom's discipline over my heart,
that they may not spare my failings
and not let their sins pass by?

So that my failings do not multiply
and my sins do not abound,
and I fall before those who oppose me,
and my enemy gloats over me.

O Lord, Father and God of my life,
do not give me lofty eyes,
and turn desire away from me.

Do not let gluttony and lust lay hold of me,
and do not hand me over to a shameless soul.

Hear, children, discipline of the mouth;
the one who keeps it will never be caught.

By his lips the sinner will be overtaken,
and the reviler and the proud will stumble by them.

Do not train your mouth to oaths,
and do not make a habit of naming the Holy One.

For as a household slave who is examined continually
will not be free of welts,
so too one who swears and names the Name at all times
will never be cleansed of sin.

There is a kind of speech clothed with death;{a}
let it not be found in the inheritance of Jacob!
For all these things will be kept far from the godly,
and they will not roll about in sins.

Do not train your mouth to coarse filthiness,
for in it is a word of sin.

Call to mind your father and your mother,
for you sit among great men,
so that you do not forget yourself in their sight
and play the fool by your habit,
and wish you had not been born,
and curse the day of your birth.

A man trained in words of reproach
will not be schooled in all his days.

Two kinds multiply sins,
and the third will bring on wrath:
a hot soul, like a blazing fire,
will not be quenched until it is swallowed up;
a man who fornicates with the body of his own flesh
will not cease until the fire burns him up.

To a fornicating man all bread is sweet;
he will not let up until he comes to his end.

A man who strays from his own bed
says in his soul, “Who sees me?
Darkness is around me, and the walls cover me,
and no one sees me; what have I to be wary of?
The Most High will not remember my sins.”

What he fears is human eyes,
and he has not grasped that the Lord's eyes
outshine the sun ten thousandfold,
gazing on all the ways of human beings
and peering into hidden corners.

Before all things were created, they were known to him,
and so also after their completion.

This man will be punished in the streets of the city,
and where he did not suspect, he will be caught.

So also a wife who leaves her husband
and produces an heir by a stranger.

She will be led out into the assembly,
and a visitation will come upon her children.

Her children will not spread into roots,
and her branches will not bear fruit.

She will leave behind her memory for a curse,
and her disgrace will not be wiped away.

notes.text: Probably blasphemy, which carried the death penalty (Lev 24:16).
GII adds a verse (23:28): “It is great glory to follow God, and to be received by him is length of days.”

verses.text:
Wisdom will sing her own soul's praise
and will boast in the midst of her people.

Within the gathering of the Most High her mouth will open,
and facing his armies she will make her boast:

“From the mouth of the Most High I came forth,
and like a mist I covered the earth.

In the heights I pitched my tent,
and my throne was in a pillar of cloud.

The vault of heaven I circled alone,
and in the depth of the abysses I walked about.

Over the sea's waves and over the whole earth,
over every people and nation, I took possession.

Among all these I sought rest:
in whose inheritance would I lodge?

Then the Creator of all things gave me command,
and the One who created me made my tent rest,
and he said, ‘In Jacob pitch your tent,
and in Israel receive your inheritance.’

Before the age, from the beginning, he created me,
and to the age I will never fail.

In the holy tent I ministered before him,
and so in Zion I was set firm.

In the beloved city he likewise gave me rest,
and in Jerusalem was my authority.

I struck root among a people given glory,
in the Lord's portion, his inheritance.

Like a cedar in Lebanon I was raised high,
and like a cypress on the mountains of Hermon.

Like a palm in En-gedi{a} I was raised high,
and like rose bushes in Jericho,
like a comely olive in the plain,
and like a plane tree I was raised high.

Like cinnamon and camel's thorn I gave off the fragrance of spices,
and like choice myrrh I spread a sweet scent,
like galbanum and onycha and stacte,
and like the vapor of frankincense in the tent.{b}

Like a terebinth I stretched out my branches,
and my branches are branches of glory and grace.

Like a vine I put forth grace,
and my blossoms became the fruit of glory and riches.

Come over to me, you who long for me,
and be filled from my produce.

For to remember me is sweeter than honey,
and to inherit me, sweeter than the comb of honey.

Those who eat me will still be hungry,
and those who drink me will still be thirsty.

The one who obeys me will not be put to shame,
and those who work by me will not sin.”

It is the law that brims with wisdom like the Pishon,{e}
and like the Tigris in the days of first fruits;

that makes understanding run over like the Euphrates,
and like the Jordan in the days of harvest;

that makes discipline shine out like light,{f}
like the Gihon in the days of vintage.

The first man did not finish knowing her,
and so the last will not track her out.

For her thinking is fuller than the sea,
and her counsel than the great abyss.

And I was like a channel out of a river,
like a watercourse into a garden.

I said, “I will water my garden
and soak my flower bed”;
and look — my channel became a river,
and my river became a sea.

Still more I will make discipline shine like the dawn,
and I will make it appear far off.

Still more I will pour out teaching like prophecy
and leave it behind for generations of the ages.

See: I have not toiled for myself alone,
but for all who seek her out.

notes.text: So some Greek witnesses (Engaddi); others read “on the beaches.”
These are the ingredients of the sacred anointing oil and incense (Exod 30:23–34).
Verses 18 and 24 are lacking in Swete's text; they belong to the longer Greek recension (GII).
Quoting Deut 33:4. Sirach is the first known writer to identify Wisdom with the Torah outright.
Pishon, Tigris, Euphrates, and Gihon are the rivers of Eden (Gen 2:10–14).
“Like light” is probably a misreading of a Hebrew word for “like the Nile” (ye'or read as 'or).

verses.text:
In three things I was made beautiful,
and I stood up in beauty before the Lord and people:{a}
harmony of brothers, and friendship of neighbors,
and wife and husband suited to each other.

Three kinds my soul hated,
and I am deeply offended at their life:
a poor man who is proud, a rich man who lies,
an old adulterer who lacks understanding.

If you did not gather in your youth,
how will you find in your old age?

How lovely is judgment in gray hair,
and for elders to know counsel!

How lovely is wisdom in the old,
and understanding and counsel in those given glory!

The crown of the old is wide experience,
and their boast is the fear of the Lord.

blessed is he who has found good sense,
and he who tells his story into listening ears.

How great is he who has found wisdom!
But none is above the one who fears the Lord.

The fear of the Lord rises above all things;
to whom will the one who holds it be likened?

[The fear of the Lord is where loving him begins,
and faith is where clinging to him begins.]{c}

Any wound, only not a wound of the heart!
Any wickedness, only not the wickedness of a wife!

Any assault, only not from those who hate!
Any vengeance, only not from enemies!

There is no head above a snake's head,{d}
and no wrath above an enemy's wrath.

I would sooner make my home with a lion and a dragon
than make my home with an evil wife.

A wife's wickedness alters her look
and darkens her face like a bear's.

Her husband takes his seat among his neighbors,
and he cannot help sighing bitterly.

Small is any wickedness beside a wife's wickedness;
may a sinner's lot fall upon her!

A sandy climb for an old man's feet —
so is a wife full of tongue to a quiet husband.

Do not fall headlong for a woman's beauty,
and do not set your longing on a woman.

There is wrath and brazenness and great disgrace
when a wife provides for her husband.

A heart brought low, a sullen face,
a wounded heart — so is an evil wife;
slack hands and buckling knees —
so is she who does not make her husband blessed.

With a woman sin made its start,{e}
and on her account we all die.

Do not give water an outlet,
or an evil wife freedom of speech.

If she does not walk at your hand,
cut her away from your flesh.{f}

notes.text: The Greek of the first line is uncertain; some witnesses read “In three things my soul took delight.”
The Hebrew, as reported, adds here “and who does not plow with an ox and an ass together” (compare Deut 22:10).
Verse 12 is lacking in Swete's text; it belongs to the longer Greek recension (GII).
The Hebrew word rosh means both “head” and “venom”; the Greek has taken the first sense.
Usually taken as a reference to Eve (Gen 3); some interpreters, as reported, take it of the evil wife of the context.
That is, divorce her (compare Deut 24:1).

verses.text:
A good wife — her husband is blessed;
the count of his days is doubled.

A brave wife gladdens her husband,
and he will fill out his years in peace.

A good wife is a good portion;
she will be given as a portion to those who fear the Lord.

Be he rich or poor, his heart is good,
and his face is cheerful in every season.

Of three things my heart was in dread,
and over the fourth I made supplication:{a}
slander in a city, a mob's gathering,
and false accusation — all are more grievous than death.

But pain of heart and mourning is a wife jealous of a wife,
and a tongue's whip that shares itself with all.

A yoke of oxen jolted about is an evil wife;
one who takes hold of her is like one gripping a scorpion.

Great wrath is a drunken wife;
she will not cover her own disgrace.

A wife's fornication shows in the lifting of her eyes,
and by her eyelids it will be known.

Over a headstrong daughter set a firm guard,
so that, finding license, she does not make use of it.

Keep watch behind a brazen eye,
and do not wonder if it offends against you.

Like a thirsty traveler she will open her mouth
and drink from any water near at hand;
she will sit down facing every peg
and open her quiver to every arrow.

A wife's grace delights her husband,
and her knowing will put fat on his bones.

A silent wife is a gift of the Lord,
and nothing can be traded for a well-schooled soul.

Grace upon grace is a modest wife,
and nothing can weigh the worth of a self-controlled soul.

As the sun rising in the heights of the Lord,
so is a good wife's beauty in the ordering of her house.

As a lamp shining on the holy lampstand,{b}
so is the beauty of a face on a steady frame.

As golden pillars on a silver base,
so are lovely legs on firm heels.

[Child, guard the bloom of your age in health,
and do not give your strength to strangers.{c}

Seek out a fertile plot from all the plain,
and sow your own seed there, trusting in your good birth.

So your offspring will survive you
and grow great, confident in their good birth.

A hired woman is reckoned as spittle,
but a married woman is a tower of death to those who use her.

A godless wife is given as the portion of a lawless man,
but a devout wife is given to one who fears the Lord.

A shameless woman wears disgrace thin,
but a modest daughter will be abashed even before her husband.

A wife without shame will be counted as a dog,
but she who has modesty will stand in fear of the Lord.

A wife who honors her husband will appear wise to all,
but one who dishonors him in her pride will be known to all as ungodly.
Blessed is the husband of a good wife,
for the count of his years will be doubled.

A wife who shouts and chatters
is like a war trumpet sounding to rout the enemy,
and every man in such a case spends his life amid the uproar of war.]

At two things my heart is grieved,
and at the third, wrath has come over me:
a fighting man in want from poverty,
and men of understanding counted as refuse,
and one who turns back from righteousness to sin —
the Lord will make him ready for the sword.

Hardly will a trader keep himself from going wrong,
and a shopkeeper will not be declared free of sin.

notes.text: So most witnesses; Swete's text has “my face was in dread.”
The lampstand of the sanctuary (Exod 25:31–40).
Verses 19–27 are lacking in Swete's text and the oldest Greek witnesses; they belong to the longer Greek recension (GII) and are found also in the Syriac, as reported.

verses.text:
Many have sinned for a thing of no account,
and one who seeks to grow rich will turn his eye away.

Between the joints of stones a peg is driven fast,
and between selling and buying sin is ground in.

If one does not hold on to the fear of the Lord with zeal,
his house will be overturned in haste.

When a sieve is shaken, the refuse stays behind;
so a man's filth stays in his reasoning.

The furnace tests the potter's vessels,
and a man's trial is in his reasoning.

Fruit lays bare the tending of a tree;
so the speech that expresses a thought lays bare a man's heart.

Before he reasons aloud, do not praise a man,
for this is the trial of people.

If you pursue what is right, you will overtake it
and put it on like a long robe of glory.

Birds will lodge with their like,
and truth will come back to those who work it.

A lion lies in ambush for prey;
so sin for those who work injustice.

The talk of a godly man is wisdom at all times,
but the fool alters like the moon.

Among the witless, watch the season,
but among the thoughtful, linger.

The talk of fools is a provocation,
and their laughter is in the wantonness of sin.

The talk of a man of many oaths makes the hair stand up,
and at their brawling one stops one's ears.

Bloodshed is the brawling of the proud,
and their abuse is a grievous hearing.

One who uncovers secrets has destroyed trust
and will never find a friend for his soul.

Hold a friend dear and keep faith with him;
but if you uncover his secrets, do not chase after him.

For as a man has destroyed his dead enemy,
so you have destroyed your neighbor's friendship.

And as a bird you let loose from your hand,
so you have let your neighbor go, and you will not hunt him down.

Do not chase him, for he is far off
and has fled like a gazelle out of the snare.

For a wound there is binding up,
and for abuse there is reconciliation,
but one who uncovers secrets has lost hope.

One who winks with the eye is crafting evil,
and no one will turn him from it.

In your sight his mouth will be sweet,
and at your words he will wonder;
but afterward he will twist his mouth
and lay a stumbling block in your words.

Many things I have hated, but nothing to match him;
and the Lord will hate him.

One who throws a stone on high throws it on his own head,
and a treacherous blow deals out wounds.

One who digs a pit will fall into it,
and one who sets a trap will be caught in it.

One who works evil — it will roll back on him,
and he will not know where it came from.

Mockery and abuse belong to the arrogant,
and vengeance lies in ambush for him like a lion.

Those who gloat at the fall of the godly will be caught in a trap,
and pain will eat them up before their death.

Wrath and anger, these too are abominations,
and the sinful man will cling to them.

One who takes vengeance will meet vengeance from the Lord,
and he will keep strict count of his sins.

Release your neighbor from the wrong he did,
and then, when you pray, your sins will be released.

Does a man keep his wrath against a man
