and seek healing from the Lord?

On a man like himself he has no mercy,
and he makes supplication about his own sins?

He, being flesh, keeps up his rage;
who will atone for his sins?

Remember the last things, and leave off enmity;
remember decay and death, and stand by the commandments.

Remember the commandments, and do not rage at your neighbor;
remember the covenant of the Most High, and overlook ignorance.

Keep away from strife, and you will make sins fewer;
for a hot-tempered man will kindle strife,

and a sinful man will throw friends into turmoil
and cast accusation among those at peace.

A hurried quarrel kindles fire,
and a hurried fight pours out blood.

Curse the whisperer and the double-tongued,
for they have destroyed many who were at peace.

A third tongue{a} has shaken many
and scattered them from nation to nation;
it has torn down strong cities
and overturned the houses of great men.

A third tongue has driven brave wives from home
and robbed them of their labors.

Whoever heeds it will find no rest
and will not make his dwelling in quiet.

The stroke of a whip makes a welt,
but the stroke of a tongue will crush bones.

Many have fallen by the sword's mouth,
yet not so many as those who have fallen by the tongue.

Blessed is he who is sheltered from it,
who has not passed through its rage,
who has not drawn its yoke
and has not been bound in its fetters.

For its yoke is an iron yoke,
and its fetters are bronze fetters.

Its death is an evil death,
and Hades is to be preferred to it.

It will not get the mastery of the godly,
and in its flame they will not be burned.

Those who abandon the Lord will fall into it,
and in them it will blaze and not be quenched;
it will be sent out on them like a lion,
and like a leopard it will maul them.

See, you hedge your property with thorns;
bind up your silver and your gold.

So make a balance and a weight for your words,
and make a door and a bar for your mouth.

Take care not to slip by it,
or you will fall before one lying in ambush.

notes.text: A Hebrew idiom for slander: the tongue of a third party that comes between two.

verses.text:
One who acts mercifully will lend to his neighbor,
and one who props him up with his hand keeps the commandments.

Lend to your neighbor in the season of his need,
and pay your neighbor back again at the proper season.

Make your word firm and keep faith with him,
and at every season you will find what you need.

Many have counted a loan as a windfall
and made trouble for those who stood by them.

Until he receives, he will kiss a man's hands,
and he will lower his voice over his neighbor's money;
but at the time for repayment he will drag out the time
and pay back words of indifference
and lay the blame on the season.

Many, then, have refused to lend, not out of wickedness;
they were afraid of being robbed for nothing.

Yet with a man in low estate be patient,
and do not make him wait on your alms.

For the commandment's sake take the part of a poor man,
and in his need do not send him away empty.

Lose silver for a brother and a friend,
and do not let it rust under a stone to be lost.

Lay up your treasure by the commands of the Most High,
and it will profit you more than gold.

Shut almsgiving up in your storehouses,
and it will rescue you from every evil;

more than a stout shield and a heavy spear,
it will fight for you in the face of the enemy.

A good man will stand surety for his neighbor,
but one who has lost his shame will abandon him.

Do not forget the favors of your guarantor,
for he gave his soul for you.
A sinner will squander the good things of his guarantor,
and one ungrateful at heart will abandon his rescuer.

Suretyship has ruined many who were prospering
and tossed them about like a wave of the sea;
it has driven men of power from their homes,
and they have wandered among foreign nations.

A sinner who falls into suretyship
and goes after business deals will fall into lawsuits.

Take your neighbor's part as far as your strength allows,
and look to yourself, so that you do not fall.

First things for life are water and bread
and clothing and a house to cover one's shame.

Better a poor man's life under a shelter of beams
than splendid fare in other people's houses.
With little or with much, be well content.

A wretched life it is to go from house to house,
and where you are a sojourner you will not open your mouth.

You will play host and pour drink to no thanks,
and on top of this you will hear bitter things:

“Come here, sojourner, set the table,
and if you have anything at hand, feed me.”

“Get out, sojourner, before one given glory;
my brother has come to lodge with me; I need the house.”

These things are hard on a man of understanding:
reproach over lodging and the scorn of the creditor.

One who loves his son will keep the whip on him,
so that he may be glad over him at the last.

One who disciplines his son will have joy of him
and will boast of him among his acquaintances.

One who teaches his son will rouse his enemy's jealousy
and will exult over him before his friends.

His father has come to his end, and it is as though he had not died,
for he has left behind one like himself.

In his life he saw and was glad,
and in his end he was not grieved.

He has left behind an avenger against his enemies
and one to repay favors to his friends.

One who pampers his son will be binding up his wounds,
and at every cry his insides will churn.

An unbroken horse turns out hard,
and a son let loose turns out headlong.

Coddle a child, and he will make you dread him;
play with him, and he will grieve you.

Do not laugh along with him, so that you do not ache along with him
and grind your teeth at the last.
Do not give him authority in his youth.{a}

Bend his neck in youth
and bruise his ribs while he is a child,
so that he does not grow hard and disobey you.

Discipline your son and work at him,
so that you do not stumble over his indecency.

Better a poor man, healthy and strong in constitution,
than a rich man whipped in his body.

Health and sound condition are better than all gold,
and a robust body than riches beyond count.

There is no wealth better than health of body
and no gladness above gladness of heart.

Better death than a bitter life,
or rest to the age than lingering sickness.

Good things poured over a closed mouth
are like portions of food laid on a grave.

What good is an offering to an idol?
For it will neither eat nor smell.
So is the one whom the Lord is pursuing:

with his eyes he looks on, and he moans,
as a eunuch moans who holds a virgin in his arms.

Do not give your soul over to grief,
and do not afflict yourself by your own counsel.

Gladness of heart is the life of a man,
and a man's exultation is length of days.

Jealousy and rage shorten days,
and worry brings old age before its season.

A bright and good heart at table
will take care over its food.{b}

notes.text: GII adds: “and do not overlook his follies.” In verse 12 the first line also comes from GII.

At this point the Greek manuscripts have suffered a transposition: in all of them, 30:25–33:13a (NRSV numbering) stands after 33:13b–36:16a. The Hebrew and the Latin preserve the original order, which is followed here, as in most modern versions. Swete prints the Greek in the transposed order; his chapter and verse numbers for this section therefore differ.

verses.text:
Wakefulness over wealth melts the flesh away,
and the worry it brings drives off sleep.

Wakeful worry will keep slumber away,
and a heavy sickness will snatch sleep off.

A rich man toils at heaping up money,
and when he rests he is filled with his delicacies.

A poor man toils at the lack of a livelihood,
and when he rests he becomes needy.

One who loves gold will not be counted righteous,
and one who pursues gain will be filled with it.{a}

Many have been handed over to ruin for the sake of gold,
and their destruction stood in front of their face.

It is a timber to trip over for those who pour out offerings to it,
and every witless man will be caught by it.

Blessed is the rich man who has been found blameless,
who has not gone running after gold.

Who is he, that we may call him blessed?
For he has done wonders among his people.

Who has been put to the proof by it and found complete?
Let it be his boast.
Who could have transgressed, and did not transgress,
and could have done evil, and did not do it?

His good things will be made firm,
and the assembly will tell over his almsgiving.

Are you seated at a great table?
Do not open your gullet over it,
and do not say, “What plenty is on it!”

Wherever he looks, do not stretch out your hand,
and do not jostle him in the dish.

Judge your neighbor's feelings from your own,
and think over every matter.

Eat, as a human being should, what is set before you,
and do not gobble, or you will be detested.

For manners' sake be the first to leave off,
and do not be greedy past filling, lest you cause offense.

And if you sit in the midst of many,
do not reach out your hand before they do.

How enough for a well-schooled man is a little!
And on his bed he does not gasp for breath.

Healthy sleep comes with a moderate stomach;
he rises early, and his soul is his own.
The pain of wakefulness and of vomiting
and of griping in the bowels is with the insatiable man.

And if you have been pressed into eating too much,
rise up, go out in the middle, and you will have rest.{c}

Hear me, child, and do not make light of me,
and in the end you will find out my words;
in all your works be brisk,
and no sickness will come near you.

One who is lavish with bread, lips will bless,
and the testimony to his goodness is to be trusted.

One who is mean with bread, the city will grumble at,
and the testimony to his meanness is exact.

Do not play the hero over wine,
for wine has destroyed many.

A furnace proves the tempering of steel by dipping;
so wine proves hearts in the quarreling of the arrogant.

Wine is like life to human beings
if you drink it in its measure.
What life is there for one who goes without wine?
It has been created for gladness to human beings.

Gladness of heart and good cheer of soul
is wine drunk in its season and to sufficiency.

Bitterness of soul is wine drunk to excess,
with provocation and stumbling.

Drunkenness swells a fool's rage to his stumbling,
cutting down strength and adding wounds.

At a banquet of wine do not reprove your neighbor,
and do not treat him with contempt in his merriment;
speak no word of reproach to him,
and do not press him with demands.

notes.text: The Greek diaphora means both “gain, profit” and “ruin”; the wordplay continues in verse 6.
An “evil eye” is a greedy or grudging eye.
The Greek is uncertain; some witnesses read “vomit” (a sense attested in the Hebrew, as reported).

verses.text:
And when you have done all your duty, recline,
so that you may be glad on their account
and receive a garland for your good order.

Speak, elder, for it is fitting for you,
but with exact knowledge,
and do not get in the way of the music.

Where there is listening, do not pour out chatter,
and do not show yourself wise out of season.

A seal of carnelian in a setting of gold —
such is a concert of music at a banquet of wine.

A seal of emerald in a mounting of gold —
such is the melody of music over pleasant wine.

Speak, young man, if there is need of you,
barely twice, if you are asked.

Sum up your speech, much in few words;
be like one who knows and yet holds his peace.

Among the great do not make yourself their equal,
and where another is speaking, do not prattle much.

Lightning hurries ahead of thunder,
and favor goes ahead of a modest man.

When the hour comes, get up and do not be the last;
run off home and do not dawdle.

There take your amusement and carry out your intentions,
yet do not sin with a proud word.

And for these things bless the One who made you
and who makes you drunk with his good things.

One who fears the Lord will accept discipline,
and those who rise early to seek him will find favor.

One who seeks the law will be filled with it,
but the hypocrite will stumble on it.

Those who fear the Lord will find judgment,
and they will kindle righteous acts like a light.

A sinful man turns reproof aside
and finds an interpretation to suit his will.

A man of counsel will not overlook a thought;
an alien and proud man does not shrink in fear.{a}

Do nothing without counsel,
and when you have acted, do not repent of it.

Do not go on a road of conflict,
and do not trip yourself on stony ground.
Do not be confident on a road without obstacles,
and from your own children be on your guard.{b}

In every work keep faith with your own soul,
for this too is the keeping of commandments.

One who keeps faith with the law pays heed to commandments,
and one who trusts in the Lord will suffer no loss.

notes.text: GII and some witnesses add “even after he has acted without counsel.” The Hebrew of this verse, as reported, differs considerably.
The Hebrew, as reported, reads “and watch your paths.”

verses.text:
No evil will meet one who fears the Lord,
but in trial he will rescue him again and again.

A wise man will not hate the law,
but one who is a hypocrite about it is like a boat in a squall.

A person of understanding will trust in the law,
and the law is trustworthy to him as an inquiry of the oracle.{a}

Get ready what you will say, and so you will be heard;
bind up your learning, and then answer.

A fool's insides are a cartwheel,
and his reasoning is like a spinning axle.

A stallion for breeding is like a friend who mocks:
he neighs under everyone who sits on him.

Why is one day set above another,
when all the light of each day in the year comes from the sun?

By the Lord's knowledge they were set apart,
and he varied the seasons and the feasts.

Some of them he lifted high and made holy,
and some of them he placed among the count of days.

And all human beings are from the ground,
and Adam was created out of earth.

In the fullness of his knowledge the Lord set them apart
and made their ways different.

Some of them he blessed and lifted high,
and some of them he made holy and brought near to himself;
some of them he cursed and brought low
and turned them out of their place.

As the potter's clay is in his hand —
all its ways are as he pleases —
so human beings are in the hand of the One who made them,
to render to them as he judges.{b}

And so look at all the works of the Most High:
two by two, one opposite the other.

And I, last of all, kept watch,
like one who gleans behind the grape-gatherers;

by the blessing of the Lord I got ahead,
and like a grape-gatherer I filled my winepress.

Take note that I have not toiled for myself alone,
but for all who seek discipline.

Hear me, you great ones of the people,
and you leaders of the assembly, give ear.

To son and wife, to brother and friend,
do not give power over you while you live;
and do not give your goods to another,
so that you do not change your mind and beg for them.

While you still live and there is breath in you,
do not trade yourself away to any flesh.

For it is better that your children ask of you
than that you look to your sons' hands.

In all your works keep the upper hand;
do not put a blemish on your glory.

On the day you finish the days of your life,
and in the season of your death, hand out your inheritance.

For a donkey, fodder and a rod and burdens;
for a household slave, bread and correction and labor.

Put your servant to work, and you will find rest;
let his hands go slack, and he will look for freedom.

Yoke and strap will bend the neck,
and for a wicked household slave, the rack and tortures.
Send him to work, so that he does not sit idle,
for idleness has taught much evil.

Set him to the works that befit him,
and if he does not obey, make his fetters heavy.
But do not go beyond measure with any flesh,
and do nothing without judgment.

If you have a household slave, let him be as yourself,
for with blood you acquired him.{c}
If you have a household slave, treat him as a brother,
for you will need him as you need your own soul.
If you do him harm and he gets up and runs away,
on what road will you look for him?

notes.text: Literally “as the asking of Delos,” i.e., an oracle; some read “the Urim” (Exod 28:30).
Here, in the order of the Greek manuscripts, the long section ending at 36:16a is followed by the section beginning at 30:25; see the note at 30:25. The Hebrew order is followed here.
“With blood” probably means “at great cost”; some take it as “of your own flesh and blood.”

verses.text:
Empty and false are the hopes of a man without understanding,
and dreams give wings to fools.

Like one grabbing at a shadow and chasing after wind
is one who holds on to dreams.

This set against that is the sight of dreams,
the likeness of a face facing a face.{a}

From something unclean, what will be cleansed?
And from something false, what will turn out true?

Divinings and omens and dreams are empty,
and the heart fancies things as a woman in labor does.

If they are not dispatched from the Most High in a visitation,
do not set your heart on them.

For dreams have led many astray,
and those who hoped in them have fallen.

Without lying the law will be fulfilled,
and wisdom in a faithful mouth is fulfillment.

A man who has wandered abroad knows many things,
and one of wide experience will tell out understanding.
One who has not been tested knows few things,
but one who has wandered will increase his cleverness.

Many things I saw in my wanderings,
and more than my words is my understanding.

Many times I was in danger even of death,
and I was kept safe because of these things.
The spirit of those who fear the Lord will live,
for their hope is set on the One who saves them.

One who fears the Lord will not shrink in dread
and will not play the coward, for he is his hope.
The soul of one who fears the Lord — how blessed it is!
To whom does he hold fast? And who is his prop?

The eyes of the Lord are on those who love him:
a mighty shelter and a strong prop,
a cover from the scorching wind and a cover from the noon sun,
a guard against stumbling and a help against falling.

He lifts up the soul and makes the eyes shine;
he gives healing, life, and blessing.
One who sacrifices from what was got by wrong — his offering is a mockery,
and the mockeries of the lawless are not welcome.

The Most High takes no pleasure in the offerings of the ungodly,
nor does he atone for sins by a multitude of sacrifices.

One who brings a sacrifice out of the goods of the poor
is like one who slaughters a son before his father's eyes.

Bread of the needy is the life of the poor;
one who robs them of it is a man of blood.
One who takes away his neighbor's living murders him,
and one who robs a hired man of his wage pours out blood.

One man raises a wall and another pulls it down:
what profit do the two have except their labor?

One prays and another curses:
whose voice will the Master hear?

One who washes after touching a dead body and touches it again —
what has he gained by his washing?{b}

Just so a man fasting over his sins
who turns round and does them over again:
who will listen when he prays?
What did his self-abasement profit him?

notes.text: That is, a dream is a mere reflection, as in a mirror.
On the purification after contact with a corpse, see Num 19:11–22.

verses.text: One who keeps the law multiplies offerings;
one who pays heed to the commandments sacrifices a peace offering.
One who repays a favor offers fine flour,
and one who does almsgiving sacrifices a praise offering.

What is pleasing to the Lord is to turn away from wickedness,
and atonement is to turn away from injustice.
Do not appear in the Lord's presence empty-handed,{a}
for all these things are for the commandment's sake.

The offering of a righteous man makes the altar rich,
and its sweet smell is before the Most High.

The sacrifice of a righteous man is acceptable,
and the memorial portion of it will not be forgotten.

With a good eye give the Lord glory,
and do not make small the first fruits of your hands.

In every gift let your face shine,
and in gladness make your tithe holy.

Give to the Most High as he has given,
with a good eye, as your hand has found.

For the Lord is one who repays,
and he will repay you sevenfold.
Do not try to bribe him, for he will not accept it,

He will not take a person's part against a poor man,
and he will hear the prayer of one who has been wronged.

He will never overlook the orphan's supplication,
or the widow when she pours out her story.
Do not a widow's tears run down her cheek,
and her outcry rise against the one who made them fall?

One who serves with good will will be accepted,
and his petition will reach to the clouds.

and gives judgment for the righteous and carries out judgment.
And the Lord will not be slow,
nor will he be patient with them,
until he has crushed the loins of the merciless

until he has paid back a man according to his doings,
and the works of human beings according to their designs;

until he has judged the cause of his people
and gladdened them with his mercy.

Mercy in the season of affliction is a lovely thing,
like clouds of rain in the season of drought.

notes.text: Exod 23:15; Deut 16:16.

verses.text: Have mercy on us, Master, God of all things, and look on us,
and cast the fear of you on all the nations.

Lift up your hand against foreign nations,
and let them see your dominion.

As in their sight you were shown holy in us,
so in our sight be shown great in them;

and let them know you, just as we too have known
that there is no God but you, Lord.
Make signs new and wonders different;
glorify your hand and your right arm.
Rouse your fury and pour out your wrath;
take away the adversary and wipe out the enemy.

Hurry on the season and remember the oath,
and let them tell out your mighty works.

Let the one who escapes be eaten up in the wrath of fire,
and those who mistreat your people find destruction.

Smash the heads of the rulers of the enemy
who say, “There is no one but us.”
Gather all the tribes of Jacob,{a}
[Not used in this numbering; see the note at verse 13.]
[Not used in this numbering; see the note at verse 13.]
and give them their inheritance as from the beginning.

Have mercy, Lord, on a people called by your name,
and on Israel, whom you made like a firstborn.{b}

Have compassion on the city of your holiness,
Jerusalem, the place of your rest.

Fill Zion with the telling of your wonders,{c}
and your people with your glory.

Give testimony to those you created at the beginning,
and raise up the prophecies spoken in your name.

Pay their wages to those who wait on you,
and let your prophets prove to be faithful.

Hear, Lord, the prayer of your suppliants,
according to Aaron's blessing over your people,{d}
and all who are on the earth will know
that you are the Lord, the God of the ages.

The belly will eat any food,
yet one food is better than another.

As the throat tries out kinds of venison,
so a discerning heart tries out false words.

A twisted heart will bring grief,
and a man of experience will pay him back.

A woman will receive any male,
yet one daughter is better than another.

A wife's beauty brightens the face
and outdoes every desire of a man.

If on her tongue there is mercy and gentleness,
her husband is not like other sons of men.

One who acquires a wife makes a start on possessions,
a help fitting for him and a pillar of rest.{e}

Where no hedge is, the property is pillaged,
and a man without a wife roams about and groans.

For who will trust a nimble robber
darting from city to city?
So too a man who has no nest
and lodges wherever evening overtakes him.

notes.text: The numbering here follows NRSV, which has no verses 14–15 in this chapter (they are kept below as empty placeholders so that the following verse numbers match NRSV); KJV and other editions number this prayer 36:1–17. In the Greek manuscripts the transposed section (see the notes at 30:25 and 33:13) ends after verse 13, and the next words resume after the displaced block.
Exod 4:22.
The Greek is uncertain; some witnesses read “Fill Zion with your praise.”

verses.text:
Every friend will say, “I too am your friend”;
but there is a friend who is a friend in name only.

Is it not a grief that comes near to death
when a companion and friend turns into an enemy?

O wicked imagining, from where did you roll in
to cover the dry land with treachery?

A companion takes pleasure in a friend's good cheer,
but in a season of affliction he will be against him.

A companion toils alongside a friend for the belly's sake,
and in the face of battle he will take up the shield.

Do not forget a friend in your soul,
and do not be unmindful of him among your riches.

Every counselor praises counsel,
but there is one who counsels toward himself.

Keep your soul guarded from a counselor,
and know beforehand what his need is —
for he will counsel for himself —
so that he does not cast a lot over you

and say to you, “Your road is good,”
and then stand at a distance to see what happens to you.

Do not take counsel with one who eyes you with suspicion,
and hide your counsel from those who envy you.

Do not consult a woman about her rival,
or a coward about war,
a merchant about bartering,
or a buyer about selling,
an envious man about gratitude,
or a merciless man about kindness,
an idler about any work,
or a hired man by the year about finishing,
a lazy household slave about much work —
do not attend to these on any matter of counsel.

But stay constantly with a godly man
whom you know to be a keeper of the commandments,
whose soul is like your own soul,
and who will grieve with you if you stumble.

And make the counsel of your heart stand firm,
for nothing is more trustworthy to you than it.

For a man's soul sometimes brings him word
better than seven lookouts sitting on high on a watchtower.

And with all these, make your prayer to the Most High
that he may make your way straight in truth.

The beginning of every work is reason,
and before every action is counsel.
As the track of the heart's turning,

four portions spring up:
good and evil, life and death,
and the tongue is master over them always.

There is a man who is clever, the teacher of many,
and yet to his own soul he is of no use.

There is a clever speaker who is hated;
he will end up stripped of every food,

for grace was not given him from the Lord,
because he is stripped of all wisdom.

There is one who is wise for his own soul,
and the fruits of his understanding are trustworthy on his lips.

A wise man will teach his own people,
and the fruits of his understanding are trustworthy.

A wise man will be filled with blessing,
and all who see him will call him blessed.

The life of a man is days that can be numbered,
but the days of Israel are past numbering.

The wise man will inherit trust among his people,
and his name will live to the age.

Child, in your life put your soul to the test,
and see what is evil for it, and do not give it that.

For not everything is profitable for everyone,
and not every soul takes pleasure in everything.

Do not be insatiable for every delicacy,
and do not pour yourself out over foods;

for with much food there will be sickness,
and excess will come near to colic.

Through excess many have died,
but the one who takes heed will add to his life.

Give the physician the honors owed him, against the times you need him,
for the Lord created him too.

For healing comes from the Most High,
and from the king he will receive a gift.

The physician's knowledge will lift up his head,
and in the sight of great men he will be admired.

The Lord created remedies out of the earth,
and a man of good sense will not spurn them.

Was not water made sweet by a piece of wood,{a}
so that his strength might be known?

And he gave human beings knowledge,
so that he might be glorified in his marvels.
By them he heals and takes away pain;

the perfumer makes a compound out of them.
His works will never be brought to an end,
and from him well-being is over the face of the earth.

Child, in your sickness do not be careless,
but pray to the Lord, and he will heal you.

Put away going astray and set your hands straight,
and cleanse your heart of every sin.

Give a sweet-smelling offering and a memorial portion of fine flour,{b}
and make your offering rich, as one who will soon be no more.

After that make room for the healer — the Lord made him as well —
and let him not go off from you, since you have need of him.
There is a season when success lies in their hands;

for they too will pray to the Lord
that he may prosper them in giving relief
and in healing, for the sake of preserving life.

One who sins in the sight of his Maker —
let him fall into the physician's hands.{c}

Child, let your tears flow over the dead,
and like one suffering terribly, start the lament;
shroud his body as is his due,
and do not neglect his burial.

Make the weeping bitter and the beating of the breast hot,
and keep up the mourning as he deserves,
a day or two, to avoid talk,
and then take comfort on account of grief.

For from grief comes death,
and grief of heart bends one's strength.

In misfortune grief also stays,
and the life of the poor man is a curse to the heart.{d}

Do not hand your heart over to grief;
send it away, remembering the end.

Do not forget, for there is no coming back;
you will not benefit him, and you will harm yourself.

Remember my sentence, for yours will be the same:
“For me yesterday, and for you today.”

When the dead man is at rest, let his memory rest,
and take comfort over him when his spirit goes out.

The wisdom of a scribe comes in the opportunity of leisure,
and one who has little business will become wise.

How will he become wise who grips the plow
and whose boast is in the shaft of a goad,
who drives oxen and is taken up with their tasks,
and whose talk is about the offspring of bulls?

He gives his heart to turning furrows,
and his wakefulness to fodder for heifers.

So the potter, sitting at his work
and spinning the wheel with his feet,
who is always set down in anxious care over his work,
and all his output is by count;

with his arm he will shape the clay,
and before his feet he will bend its stiffness;
he will give his heart to completing the glaze,
and his wakefulness to cleaning out the kiln.

All these put their trust in their hands,
and each one is wise in his own work.

Without them no city will be lived in,
and people will not sojourn or walk about there.

they will not bring discipline and judgment to light,
and among the parables they will not be found.
Yet they keep the fabric of the age firm,
and their prayer is in the work of their craft.
How different the one who gives his soul
and ponders the law of the Most High!

notes.text: Lev 2:1–2. The last phrase is obscure in the Greek.
The Hebrew, as reported, reads “will behave proudly before the physician.”
The Greek of this verse is obscure.
Literally “renews his ear”; the Greek is uncertain.

verses.text:
He will seek out the wisdom of all the ancients
and be taken up with prophecies;

he will keep the narratives of men of renown
and will go into the twists of parables;

he will seek out the hidden things of proverbs
and will busy himself with the riddles of parables.

He will serve in the midst of great men
and appear before a ruler;
he will travel through the land of foreign nations,
for he has put good and evil among human beings to the test.

He will give his heart to rising early
to the Lord who made him,
and before the Most High he will make his petition;
he will open his mouth in prayer
and make supplication about his sins.

If the great Lord so wills,
he will be filled with a spirit of understanding;
he will pour out sayings of his wisdom like rain
and in prayer give thanks to the Lord.

He will set straight his counsel and knowledge
and ponder the Lord's hidden things.

He will bring to light the discipline of his teaching
and will boast in the law of the Lord's covenant.

Many will praise his understanding,
and to the age it will not be wiped out;
his memory will not depart,
and his name will live from generation to generation.

His wisdom the nations will recount,
and his praise the congregation will announce.

If he stays on, he will leave a name greater than a thousand;
and if he goes to his rest, that is enough for him.

Still more I will tell, having thought it through,
for I am filled up like the moon at the full.

Listen to me, holy children, and bud
like a rose growing beside a stream in the field;

Give his name majesty
and acknowledge him with his praise,
with songs of the lips and with harps,
and say this in your acknowledgment:

“The works of the Lord are all very good,
and every command of his will happen in its season.

No one may say, ‘What is this? Why is this?’
for all things will be sought out in their season.
At his word the water stood like a heap,{a}
and at the utterance of his mouth, the reservoirs of waters.

At his command all his good pleasure is done,
and there is no one who will lessen his saving work.

The works of all flesh are before him,
and nothing can be hidden from his eyes.

From age to age he looks on,
and nothing is a marvel before him.

No one may say, ‘What is this? Why is this?’
for all things have been created for their uses.

His blessing has covered the dry land like a river
and soaked it like a flood.

Even so the nations will inherit his wrath,
as he turned waters into salt.{b}

His ways are level for the holy;
even so they are stumbling blocks for the lawless.

Good things were created for the good from the beginning,
even so evil things for sinners.

The chief of every need for the life of a human being
is water and fire and iron and salt
and the finest of wheat flour, and milk and honey,
the blood of the grape and oil and clothing.

All these are for good to the godly;{c}
even so for sinners they will be turned to evil.

There are winds that have been created for vengeance,
and in their fury they have made their whips firm;
in the season of the end they will pour out their strength
and will calm the wrath of the One who made them.

Fire and hail and famine and death,
all these have been created for vengeance;

the teeth of wild beasts, and scorpions and vipers,
and a sword avenging the ungodly to their destruction.

They will be glad at his command,
and they will be made ready on earth for their uses,
and in their seasons they will not go beyond his word.”

So from the beginning I was made firm,
and I thought it over and left it in writing:

“Good, every one, are the Lord's doings,
and each need in its hour he will furnish.

And no one may say, ‘This is worse than that,’
for all things will prove worthy in their season.”

And now with all your heart and mouth sing a song of praise
and bless the name of the Lord.

notes.text: Perhaps an allusion to the Dead Sea and the overthrow of Sodom (Gen 19).

The Masada Hebrew scroll (MasSir), copied in the first century BC, preserves portions of the text from 39:27 to 44:17, as reported. It agrees closely with Cairo Geniza manuscript B, showing that the medieval Hebrew manuscripts largely preserve the ancient Hebrew text.

verses.text:
Great preoccupation has been created for every human being,
and a heavy yoke is on the sons of Adam,
from the day of their coming out of their mother's womb
until the day of their return to the mother of all.{a}

Their reasonings and the fear of their heart:
the thought of what they wait for, the day of their end.

From the one who sits upon a throne in glory
to the one brought low in earth and ashes,

from the one who wears purple and a crown
to the one wrapped in raw linen —

there is rage and jealousy and turmoil and unsteadiness
and fear of death and wrath and strife;
and in the season of rest upon the bed
night's sleep alters his knowledge.

A little, as good as nothing, he spends in rest,
and after that, in sleep, as by day on watch,
he is thrown into turmoil by the vision of his heart,
like one who has escaped from the face of battle.

In the moment of his need he wakes
and marvels that his fear was nothing.

With all flesh, from human being to beast,
and upon sinners sevenfold more,

come death and blood and strife and sword,
calamities, famine and crushing and the scourge.

For the lawless all these were created,
and on their account the flood came.

Whatever is out of the ground goes back to the ground,
and what is out of the waters goes back into the sea.

Every gift that bribes, every wrong, will be blotted out,
while faithfulness stands through the age.

The goods of the unrighteous will dry up like a river
and will die away like a great thunderclap in a rain.

When he opens his hands, he will be glad;{b}
even so transgressors will come to utter failure.

The offspring of the ungodly will not multiply branches,
and unclean roots are on the face of sheer rock.

The sedge on every water and riverbank
will be pulled up before any grass.

Kindness is like a garden in blessings,
and almsgiving stays to the age.

The life of one who is self-sufficient and of one who works will be made sweet,
but above them both is one who finds a treasure.

Children and the building of a city make a name firm,
but above them both a blameless wife is counted.

Wine and music gladden the heart,
but above them both is the love of wisdom.

Flute and harp make melody sweet,
but above them both is a pleasant tongue.

Grace and beauty the eye will long for,
but above them both, the green of a sown field.

Friend and companion meet in season,
but above them both, a wife with her husband.

Brothers and help are for a time of affliction,
but above them both, almsgiving will rescue.

Gold and silver will set the foot firm,
but above them both counsel is prized.

Money and strength will lift up the heart,
but above them both is the fear of the Lord.
In the fear of the Lord there is no lack,
and there is no need to seek help with it.

The fear of the Lord is like a garden of blessing,
and it covers him above all glory.

Child, do not live the life of a beggar;
better to die than to go begging.

A man who looks to someone else's table —
his life is not to be counted as life;
he will defile his soul with someone else's foods,
but a man of understanding and discipline will be on his guard.

In the mouth of the shameless, begging will be sweet,
but in his belly a fire will burn.

notes.text: That is, the earth (compare Gen 3:19).
The Greek of this line is obscure.

verses.text:
O death, how bitter is the remembrance of you
to a man living at peace among his possessions,
to a man who has no distractions and prospers in everything
and still has strength to take food!

O death, your sentence is good
to a man in need and failing in strength,
in extreme old age and distracted about everything,
who is contrary and has lost patience!

Do not dread the sentence of death;
remember those who went before you and those who come after.

This is the sentence from the Lord for all flesh,
and why do you refuse the good pleasure of the Most High?
Whether ten or a hundred or a thousand years,
there is no reproach about life in Hades.

Abominable children become the children of sinners,
and they frequent the dwellings of the ungodly.

The inheritance of sinners' children will perish,
and with their offspring reproach will continue.

Children will lay the blame on an ungodly father,
for on his account they are reproached.

Woe to you, ungodly men,
who have forsaken the law of God Most High!

If you are born, you will be born for a curse,
and if you die, a curse will be your portion.{a}

All things that are from the earth will return to the earth;
so the ungodly go from curse to destruction.

People mourn over their bodies,
but the name of sinners, which is not good, will be wiped out.

Take thought for your name, for it will stay with you
longer than a thousand great treasures of gold.

A good life has a number of days,
but a good name stays to the age.

Keep discipline in peace, children.
Wisdom hidden away and treasure out of sight —
what profit is there in either?

Better a man who hides his folly
than a man who hides his wisdom.

Be ashamed before father and mother of fornication,
and before a ruler and a mighty man of a lie;

before a judge and a ruler of an offense,
before the assembly and the people of lawlessness;

of meddling with his servant girl —
do not stand over her bed;
before friends, of words of reproach —
after you have given, do not reproach.

notes.text: The Greek of this verse is uncertain; the Hebrew, as reported, differs.
That is, bad manners at table; the Hebrew, as reported, differs.

subheads.15: The Works of God in Creation

verses.text:
Be ashamed of repeating a word you have heard
and of laying bare secret words;
and you will be truly modest
and find favor in the sight of every person.
Of these things do not be ashamed,
and do not show partiality and so sin:

of the law of the Most High and the covenant,
and of judgment that acquits the ungodly;{a}

of reckoning with a partner and with fellow travelers,
and of giving a share of the inheritance of companions;

of strictness with balance and with weight stones,
of getting much or getting little;

of profit from selling to merchants,
of much discipline of children,
and of making the side of a wicked household slave bleed.

Over a wicked wife a seal is good,
and where there are many hands, lock things up.

Whatever you hand over, let it be by count and weight,
and put all giving and receiving in writing.

Do not be ashamed of disciplining the senseless and the fool,
or the very old man contending with the young;
and you will be truly well schooled
and approved in the sight of all the living.

A daughter is a hidden wakefulness for a father,
and worry over her drives away sleep:
in her youth, lest she pass her prime,
and when she has married, lest she be hated;

in her virginity, lest she be defiled
and become pregnant in her father's house;
when she has a husband, lest she transgress,
and when she is married, lest she be barren.

Over a headstrong daughter keep a firm guard,
so that she does not make you a laughingstock to your enemies,
a byword in the city and the talk of the people,
and shame you before the crowd.{b}

Do not look at anyone for beauty,
and do not sit in the midst of women;

for from clothing comes the moth,
and from a woman a woman's wickedness.

Better a man's wickedness than a woman who does good;
and a woman brings shame to the point of reproach.{c}

The sun that gives light looks down on all things,
and the Lord's work is full of his glory.

The Lord has not given his holy ones power
to tell out all his marvels,
which the Lord Almighty has made firm
so that the whole might stand fast in his glory.

He tracked out the abyss and the heart,
and he saw through their cunning devices;
for the Most High knows all knowledge
and looks into the sign of the age,

declaring what has passed and what will be,
and uncovering the tracks of hidden things.

No thought slips past him;
not one word is hidden from him.

He has set in order the majestic works of his wisdom,
he who is before the age and to the age;
nothing has been added and nothing taken away,
and he had no need of any counselor.

How desirable are all his works,
down to a spark, to look upon!

All these live and stay to the age,
for all their uses, and all obey him.

All things are in pairs, one opposite the other,
and he has made nothing that falls short.

One thing confirms the good of another,
and who will have enough of gazing on his glory?

notes.text: The sense is “of giving just judgment, even if it acquits an ungodly man.”
The Hebrew, as reported, adds lines about her room having no lattice window or view of the entrance.
This harsh saying is variously rendered; the Hebrew text, as reported, is partly damaged here.
The Hebrew, as reported, adds “and his favor carried out his decree.”

verses.text:
The pride of the heights is the firmament in its clearness,
the look of heaven in a sight of glory.

The sun, when it appears, makes proclamation as it goes out:
a marvelous vessel, the work of the Most High.

At its noon it dries up the land,
and before its burning heat who will stand?

Great is the Lord who made it,
and at his words it speeds on its course.

And the moon too, in all things in its season,
is a proclaiming of times and a sign of the age.

From the moon comes the sign of a feast day,
a light that wanes when it is complete.

The month is named after it,{a}
growing marvelously in its changing,
a vessel of the hosts on high,
shining out in the firmament of heaven.

The beauty of heaven is the glory of the stars,
an ornament giving light in the heights of the Lord.

At the words of the Holy One they stand in their ordered place,
and they will not grow slack in their watches.

Look at the rainbow and bless the One who made it;
it is very beautiful in its brightness.

It circles the heaven with a ring of glory;
the hands of the Most High have stretched it out.

By his command he makes the snow come swiftly
and speeds the lightnings of his judgment.

Because of this the storehouses are opened,
and clouds fly out like birds.

In his majesty he made clouds strong,
and hailstones are broken off.{b}

At his appearing, mountains will be shaken;
by his will the south wind will blow.

The voice of his thunder rebukes the earth,
and so does the storm from the north and the whirlwind.
Like birds settling, he sprinkles the snow,
and its coming down is like locusts alighting.

The eye marvels at the beauty of its whiteness,
and the heart is amazed at its falling.

Hoarfrost he scatters over the earth as if it were salt,
and as it hardens it grows into thorn-tips.

A chill wind blows from the north,
and crystal ice hardens over the water;
upon every pooling of water it comes to rest,
and the water dons it as a breastplate.

It will eat up the mountains and burn the wilderness
and quench green growth like fire.

A healing for all things is a mist coming swiftly;
dew, meeting the burning heat, will bring cheer.

By his reasoning he calmed the abyss
and planted islands in it.

Those who sail the sea tell of its danger,
and when we hear it with our ears we marvel.

In it are strange and marvelous works,
variety of every living thing,
the creation of sea monsters.

Because of him his messenger has success,{c}
and by his word all things hold together.

Many things we might say and not reach the end,
and the sum of our words is: “He is the All.”{d}

Where shall we find strength to glorify him?
For he is the Great One above all his works.

The Lord is to be feared and is exceedingly great,
and marvelous is his dominion.

Who has seen him and will describe him?
And who will make him great as he is?

Many hidden things are greater than these,
for we have seen few of his works.

For the Lord made all things,
and to the godly he gave wisdom.

notes.text: In Hebrew, “month” (chodesh) and “renew” (chiddesh) are related words; the Greek mēn (month) and mēnē (moon) keep a similar play.
In verses 15–17 the order of lines differs between Hebrew and Greek, and modern versions rearrange them following the Hebrew; the Greek order is kept here.
Or “his journey reaches its end”; the Greek is uncertain.
Greek to pan. The Hebrew, as reported, reads “He is everything” (hu' hakkol).

verses.text:
Let us now praise men of glory,{a}
our fathers in their generations.

Great glory the Lord created in them,
his majesty from the age.

There were those who held lordship in their kingdoms
and men named for their might,
giving counsel by their understanding,
announcing things in prophecies;

those who sought out tunes of music
and set out poems in writing;

rich men, furnished with strength,
living in peace in their dwellings —

all these were glorified in their generations
and were a boast in their days.

There are some of them who have left a name behind them,
so that their praises are told.

Others there are of whom no memorial exists;
they are gone as if they never were,
they became like ones never born,
and so did their children after them.

But these were men of mercy,
whose righteous deeds have not been forgotten;

with their offspring a good inheritance will remain,
their descendants within the covenants.

Their offspring stand within the covenants,
and their children likewise, for their sake.

To the age their offspring will remain,
and their glory will not be wiped out.

Their bodies were buried in peace,
and their name lives to generations.

Peoples will tell out their wisdom,
and the assembly proclaims their praise.

Enoch pleased the Lord and was taken across,{b}
an example of repentance to generations.

Covenants of the age were set with him,
that all flesh should not again be wiped out by a flood.

Great father of a throng of nations was Abraham;
none has turned up to equal him in glory;

For this he made it firm to him by oath
that in his seed nations should be blessed,
that he would make him many as earth's dust
and raise his seed on high as the stars are,
and make them heirs from sea to sea,
from the River to the ends of the land.

With Isaac too he set it so,
for the sake of Abraham his father.

The blessing of all people and the covenant
he made to rest on the head of Jacob;
he acknowledged him in his blessings
and gave him the land as an inheritance;
he marked out its portions
and divided them among twelve tribes.
And out of him he brought forth a man of mercy,
who found favor in the eyes of all flesh,

notes.text: So the heading in the Greek manuscripts (Paterōn hymnos); in the Hebrew, as reported, “Praise of the Fathers of Old.” The hymn runs through chapter 50.
Gen 5:24. The Hebrew of Geniza MS B, as reported, reads “a sign of knowledge”; the Masada scroll, as reported, lacks this verse.
Gen 6:9. The Masada scroll's text breaks off at about this point, as reported.

verses.text:
beloved by God and by human beings,
Moses, whose memorial is in blessings.

He made him like the holy ones in glory{a}
and made him great in the terrors he brought on his enemies.

In his faithfulness and meekness he made him holy;{c}
he chose him out of all flesh.

He let him hear his voice
and led him into the thick darkness
and gave him commandments face to face,
a law of life and knowledge,
to teach Jacob the covenant
and Israel his judgments.

He lifted up Aaron, a holy man like him,
his brother, of the tribe of Levi.

He set up an everlasting covenant for him
and gave him the priesthood of the people;
he blessed him with comeliness
and girded him with a robe of glory.

And he surrounded him with pomegranates,
with very many golden bells all around,
to give out a sound as he walked,
to make a sound heard in the temple
as a memorial for the sons of his people;

with a crown of gold upon the turban,
an engraving of a seal of holiness,{f}
a boast of honor, a work of might,
the desires of the eyes, richly adorned.

Before him there were never such lovely things;
to the age no outsider has put them on,
but only his sons
and his descendants perpetually.

His sacrifices shall be wholly burned,
twice every day continually.{g}

He chose him out of all the living
to bring an offering to the Lord,
incense and a sweet smell as a memorial portion,
to make atonement for your people.

He gave him, in his commandments,
authority in covenants of judgments,
to teach Jacob the testimonies
and to give light to Israel in his law.

Outsiders conspired against him
and envied him in the wilderness,
the men around Dathan and Abiram
and the band of Korah, in fury and wrath.{i}

The Lord saw it and was not pleased,
and they were brought to an end in the fury of his wrath;
he worked wonders against them,
to consume them in the flame of his fire.

for they eat the sacrifices of the Lord,
which he gave to him and to his offspring.

Therefore a covenant of peace was set up for him,
to be leader of the sanctuary and of his people,
that to him and to his offspring should belong
the greatness of the priesthood to the ages.

May he give you wisdom in your heart
to judge his people in righteousness,
so that their good things may not vanish,
and their glory for their generations.

notes.text: “The holy ones” are the angels; the Hebrew, as reported, reads “like God” (Exod 7:1).
That is, the Urim and Thummim (Exod 28:30), which the Greek renders “manifestations and truth.”
The plate inscribed “Holy to the Lord” (Exod 28:36).
A Hebrew idiom for ordaining a priest (Lev 8).
Num 16.

verses.text:
Mighty in war was Joshua{a} son of Nun,
the successor of Moses in prophecies,
who became, as his name means,
great for the saving of God's chosen,
to take vengeance on enemies who rose up,
so that he might give Israel its inheritance.

How glorified he was when he lifted his hands
and stretched out the sword against cities!{b}

Who stood so firm before him?
For he waged the wars of the Lord.

Was it not by his hand that the sun stood back,
so that a single day was made two?{c}

He called on the Most High, the Mighty One,
when enemies pressed on him from every side,
and the great Lord heard him
with hailstones of overwhelming power.

He dashed down upon the nation in war,
and on the descent he destroyed those who stood against him,
so that the nations might know his full armor,
that his war was before the Lord;
for he followed after the Mighty One.

And in the days of Moses he did a deed of mercy,
he and Caleb son of Jephunneh:
they stood against the assembly,
held the people back from sin,
and stopped the murmuring of wickedness.{d}

These two alone were kept safe
out of six hundred thousand men on foot,
to bring them into their inheritance,
into a land flowing with milk and honey.

And the Lord gave Caleb strength,
and it stayed with him until old age,
so that he went up onto the heights of the land,
and his offspring held it as an inheritance,{e}

so that all the sons of Israel might see
that it is good to follow after the Lord.

And the judges, each by his own name,
whose heart did not go whoring
and who did not turn away from the Lord —
may their memory be in blessings!

May their bones sprout again from their place,
and may their name be renewed in the sons of those who were glorified.

Beloved by his Lord,
Samuel, the prophet of the Lord, established a kingdom
and anointed rulers over his people.

By the law of the Lord he judged the assembly,
and the Lord watched over Jacob.

By his faithfulness he was proved an exact prophet,
and by his words he was known to be a trustworthy seer.

And the Lord thundered from heaven,
and with a great roar he made his voice heard;

and he wiped out the leaders of the Tyrians{g}
and all the rulers of the Philistines.

notes.text: Greek Iēsous Nauē. The name Joshua (Yehoshua) means “the Lord saves.”
So the Greek; the Hebrew, as reported, reads “of the enemy” (the words for “Tyre” and “enemy” look alike in Hebrew).
1 Sam 12:3–5. “Sandals” follows the Greek and Hebrew (compare 1 Sam 12:3 in the Greek).

verses.text:
After him Nathan rose up
to prophesy in the days of David.

As the fat is set apart from the peace offering,{a}
so David was set apart from the sons of Israel.

With lions he played as with young goats,
and with bears as with lambs of the flock.{b}

In his youth did he not kill a giant
and take away the people's reproach,
when he lifted his hand with a stone in the sling
and brought down the boasting of Goliath?

For he called on the Lord Most High,
and he gave strength to his right hand
to remove a man mighty in war
and to raise up the horn of his people.

In every work of his he gave thanks
to the Holy One, the Most High, with a word of glory;
with all his heart he sang songs of praise,
and he loved the One who made him.

He set singers before the altar,
to make sweet melodies by their voices.{d}

He gave the feasts their comeliness
and set the seasons in order to completion,
while they praised his holy name
and the sanctuary rang out from early morning.

After him a wise son rose up,
who on his account lived in broad security.

Solomon reigned in days of peace,
and God gave him rest all around,
so that he might set up a house for his name
and prepare a sanctuary to the age.

How wise you were in your youth,
and you were filled with understanding like a river!

Your soul covered the earth,
and you filled it with parables of riddles.

To islands far away your name went out,
and for your peace you were beloved.

At your songs, your proverbs, your parables,
and your interpretations the lands were amazed.{f}

In the name of the Lord God,
who is called the God of Israel,
you gathered gold like tin
and heaped up silver like lead.

Yet you set your loins down beside women
and gave them dominion over your body.{g}

so that the sovereignty was split in two,
and out of Ephraim a disobedient kingdom ruled.

And Solomon went to rest with his fathers
and left behind him one of his offspring,
broad in folly and lacking understanding,
Rehoboam,{i} who turned the people away by his counsel.
And Jeroboam son of Nebat, who made Israel sin,
and gave Ephraim a way of sin —

and their sins multiplied exceedingly,
so as to remove them from their land.{j}

For they sought out every wickedness,
until vengeance came upon them.

notes.text: 1 Chr 16:4–6; 25:1–7. GII adds “and daily they sing his praises in their songs.”
So some Greek witnesses; others read “and they were grieved.”
A pun in the Hebrew, as reported: Rehoboam, “the people is broad,” is called “broad in folly” (rechab 'ivvelet). See 1 Kgs 12.

verses.text:
Then a prophet arose like fire, Elijah,
whose word blazed like a lamp.{a}

He brought a famine upon them,
and by his zeal he made them few.

By the word of the Lord he shut up the heaven;
so too he brought down fire three times.{b}

How glorified you were, Elijah, in your wonders!
And who has a boast like yours?

A corpse you roused out of death,
out of Hades, at the word of the Most High;{c}

you brought kings down to destruction
and men held in glory from their beds;

you heard rebuke at Sinai
and judgments of vengeance at Horeb;{d}

you anointed kings for repayment
and prophets as successors after you;

you were taken up in a whirlwind of fire,
in a chariot with horses of fire;{e}

you are written down as ready for reproofs at the appointed times,
to calm wrath before it breaks into fury,
to turn the heart of the father to the son
and to restore the tribes of Jacob.{f}

Elijah was covered over by a whirlwind,
and Elisha was filled with his spirit;
in his days he was not shaken by any ruler,
and no one brought him under subjection.

No word was too hard for him,
and even when he had fallen asleep, his body prophesied.{h}

In his life he did wonders,
and in his death his works were marvelous.

In all this the people did not repent,
and they did not depart from their sins,
until they were carried off as plunder from their land
and scattered over all the earth.
And the people were left very few,
and a ruler from the house of David.

Some of them did what was pleasing,
and some multiplied sins.

Then their hearts and their hands shook,
and they writhed like women giving birth.

And they called on the Lord who is merciful,
spreading out their hands to him;
and the Holy One heard them quickly from heaven
and redeemed them by the hand of Isaiah.

He struck the camp of the Assyrians,
and his angel wiped them out.{k}

For Hezekiah did what was pleasing to the Lord
and held firmly to the ways of David his father,
which Isaiah the prophet commanded,
who was great and trustworthy in his vision.

In his days the sun went backward,
and he added life to the king.{l}

With a mighty spirit he looked on the last days
and gave comfort to the mourners of Zion.{m}

To the age he showed the things that were to be,
and the hidden things before they came.

notes.text: Mal 4:5–6 (3:23–24 in Hebrew); Isa 49:6.
The Greek of this verse is uncertain, and the Hebrew, as reported, is damaged here.
2 Kgs 20:20; 2 Chr 32:30. Hezekiah's tunnel in Jerusalem, about 1,750 feet (533 m) long, survives with its Siloam inscription.

verses.text:
The memory of Josiah is like a blending of incense
prepared by the work of a perfumer;
in every mouth it will be sweet as honey,
and like music at a banquet of wine.

He was set straight in the turning back of the people{a}
and took away the abominations of lawlessness.

He set his heart straight toward the Lord;
in the days of the lawless he made godliness strong.

Except for David and Hezekiah and Josiah,
all committed fault upon fault,
for they forsook the law of the Most High;
the kings of Judah came to an end.

For they gave their horn to others
and their glory to a foreign nation,

who set on fire the chosen city of the sanctuary
and made her streets desolate,

as foretold by the hand of Jeremiah; for they mistreated him,
and yet he had been made holy in the womb as a prophet,
to root up and to afflict and to destroy,
and likewise to build and to plant.{b}

Ezekiel saw the vision of glory,
which he showed him above the chariot of the cherubim.{c}

For he remembered the enemies in a rainstorm,{d}
and did good to those who made their ways straight.

And of the twelve prophets{e}
may the bones sprout again from their place,
for they comforted Jacob
and redeemed them in the faithfulness of hope.

How shall we make Zerubbabel great?
He too was like a signet ring on the right hand,{f}

Great too is the memory of Nehemiah,
who raised up our fallen walls for us
and set up gates and bars
and raised up our ruined houses.{h}

No one has been created on the earth like Enoch,
for he was taken up from the earth.{i}

Shem and Seth were glorified among human beings,
and above every living thing in creation is Adam.

notes.text: Ezek 1; 10.
The Greek is obscure (compare Ezek 13:11–13; 38:22). The Hebrew, as reported, reads “he also mentioned Job” (Ezek 14:14, 20); the Hebrew words for “enemy” ('oyeb) and “Job” ('iyyob) look alike.
The Twelve (Minor) Prophets, Hosea to Malachi, already counted as one collection.
Ezra 3:2, 8–13; Hag 1:12–15. Greek Iēsous.
Neh 2–7. Ezra is not named in the hymn.

verses.text:
by him the foundation was laid for the double height,
the lofty retaining wall of the temple enclosure.

In his days a cistern for water was dug,
a reservoir like the sea in its circumference.

He took thought for his people against their fall
and made the city strong against siege.

How glorified he was in the turning of the people{b}
as he came out from the house of the veil!

Like the morning star in the midst of a cloud,
like the moon at the full in its days,

like the sun shining on the temple of the Most High,
and like the rainbow giving light amid clouds of glory,

like a bloom of roses in the days of new fruits,
like lilies at an outflow of water,
like a green shoot of Lebanon on summer days,

like fire and frankincense on the censer,
like a vessel of hammered gold
adorned with every precious stone,

like an olive putting out its fruit,
and like a cypress raised high among the clouds.

When he took up his robe of boasting
and put on the perfection of boasting,
in going up to the holy altar
he made the precinct of the sanctuary glorious.

all the sons of Aaron in their glory,
with the Lord's offering in their hands,
before the whole assembly of Israel.

Finishing the service at the altars
and setting in order the offering to the Most High, the Almighty,

he stretched out his hand to the cup
and poured a libation of the blood of the grape;
he poured it out at the foundations of the altar,
a sweet smell to the Most High, the King of all.

Then all the people together hurried
and fell on their faces on the ground
to worship their Lord,
the Almighty, God Most High.

And the singers gave praise with their voices;
in the great house they made sweet melody.{c}

And the people entreated the Lord Most High
with prayer in the presence of the Merciful One,
till the Lord's worship was fully ordered
and his service was brought to completion.

Then, coming down, he raised his hands
over all the assembly of Israel's sons,
to pronounce the Lord's blessing with his lips
and glory in his name;{d}

and again they bent low in worship,
to take the blessing from the Most High.

And now bless the God of all,
who everywhere does great things,
who lifts up our days from the womb
and deals with us according to his mercy.

May he give us gladness of heart,
and may there be peace in our days in Israel,
as in the days of the age.

May he entrust his mercy to us,
and in our days may he redeem us.{e}

With two nations my soul is vexed,
and the third is not a nation:

those who dwell on the mountain of Samaria,{f} and the Philistines,
and the foolish people that dwells in Shechem.

Instruction in understanding and knowledge
I have written in this book,
Jesus son of Sirach, Eleazar, of Jerusalem,{g}
who poured out wisdom like rain from his heart.

Blessed is the one who occupies himself with these things,
and the one who lays them on his heart will become wise.

For if he does them, he will be strong for all things,
for the light of the Lord is his track.{h}

notes.text: Simon II, high priest about 219–196 BC; Ben Sira probably knew him. The Hebrew, as reported, reads “Simon son of Johanan.”
Probably the Day of Atonement (Lev 16), when the high priest came out from the holy of holies; some take it of the daily offering.
So the Greek, as best it can be read; the line is obscure.
The priestly blessing of Num 6:24–26, in which, according to later Jewish tradition (as reported), the high priest pronounced the divine name in the temple.

The Hebrew, as reported, reads instead: “May his steadfast love abide with Simon, and may he keep for him the covenant of Phinehas,” a prayer for the high-priestly line that the Greek translator, writing after that line had lost the office, made general.
The Hebrew, as reported, reads “Seir” (Edom). The “foolish people” in Shechem are the Samaritans.
The Greek manuscripts vary on the name; the Hebrew, as reported, reads “Simeon son of Jeshua son of Eleazar son of Sira.”
GII adds “and to the godly he has given wisdom. Blessed be the Lord to the age. So be it, so be it.”

subheads.1: A Prayer of Jesus son of Sirach

verses.text:
from choking fire on every side,
and from the midst of a fire I had not kindled,

from the depth of the belly of Hades,
from an unclean tongue and a lying word —

the slander of an unrighteous tongue to the king.
My soul drew near to death,
and my life was near to Hades below.

They surrounded me on every side, and there was no one to help;
I looked for the help of human beings, and there was none.

And I remembered your mercy, Lord,
and your working from the age,
that you rescue those who wait for you
and save them from the hand of their enemies.

And I lifted up my supplication from the earth
and prayed for rescue from death.

for you saved me from destruction
and rescued me from an evil time.
Therefore I will give thanks and praise you
and bless the name of the Lord.{b}

While I was still young, before I went wandering,
I sought wisdom openly in my prayer.{c}

Before the temple I asked for her,
and to the very end I will seek her out.

I bent my ear a little and received her,
and I found much discipline for myself.

I made progress in her;
to the One who gives me wisdom I will give glory.

For I resolved to put her into practice,
and I was zealous for the good, and I will never be put to shame.

My soul wrestled with her,
and in my doing of the law I was exact;
I spread out my hands to the height
and mourned over my ignorance of her.

I set my soul straight toward her,
and in purity I found her.
With her I gained a heart from the beginning;
therefore I will never be forsaken.

My insides were stirred to seek her;
therefore I have gained a good possession.

The Lord gave me a tongue as my reward,
and with it I will praise him.

Draw near to me, you who are unschooled,
and lodge in my house of instruction.{d}

Why do you say you lack these things,
and your souls are so very thirsty?

I opened my mouth and spoke:
Gain her for yourselves without money.

See with your eyes that I toiled little
and found much rest for myself.

Get a share of discipline with a large sum of silver,
and you will gain much gold by her.

May your soul be glad in his mercy,
and may you never be put to shame in praising him.

Do your work before the appointed time,
and in his time he will give you your wage.{e}

notes.text: So the Greek; the Hebrew, as reported, reads “I exalted the Lord: ‘You are my Father.’”

After this verse Cairo Geniza MS B, as reported, has a litany of sixteen lines modeled on Ps 136 (“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his steadfast love is to the age”), including thanks to the one “who makes a horn sprout for the house of David” and “who chose the sons of Zadok to be priests.” It is absent from the Greek and the Syriac.

Verses 13–30 form an alphabetic acrostic in the Hebrew. The Qumran Psalms Scroll (11QPs-a, first century AD) preserves 51:13–20 and the end of verse 30, as reported, as a separate poem among the Psalms of David, in a form with bolder bridal imagery than the Greek or Geniza MS B; many scholars hold that MS B's text of these verses is partly a retranslation or reworking. The other Qumran Sirach manuscript, 2Q18 (2QSir), preserves fragments of chapter 6, not of this poem.
The first known use of the expression, in Hebrew, as reported, beth midrash, the later name for a house of study.
Some Greek manuscripts end with the subscription “Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach.”
